questions.question: Which domain contains the flowering plant Haemanthus albiflos? A Archaea B Bacteria C Eukarya D Prokaryota.
questions.answer: C Eukarya
steps: Plants are multicellular eukaryotes: their cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotic domains, so A and B are ruled out.
Prokaryota is not one of the three domains, so D is wrong.
The answer is C, Eukarya.

questions.question: Describe the evidence Carl Woese used to support the three-domain system.
questions.answer: He compared ribosomal RNA (rRNA) base sequences between organisms.
steps: Woese compared the base sequences of ribosomal RNA from many different organisms.
rRNA is found in all cells and changes slowly, so it shows evolutionary relationships.
Organisms with more similar sequences are more closely related.
The rRNA differences showed three separate lineages: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.

questions.question: Explain the function of a pollen tube in fertilisation of flowering plants.
questions.answer: It grows down the style to the ovule and carries male nuclei to the egg cell.
steps: The pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube.
The tube grows down through the style towards the ovule.
It carries the male gamete nuclei from the pollen grain.
This delivers male nuclei to the egg so fertilisation can happen without needing water.

questions.question: Using the graph of mean pollen tube length against Verapamil concentration, determine the effect of Verapamil concentration on pollen tube growth.
questions.answer: As Verapamil concentration increases, the mean pollen tube length decreases: from about 680 um with none to about 62 um at 200 ug cm^-3 (about 91% shorter).
steps: With no Verapamil the mean pollen tube length is about 680 um, and at 1 ug cm^-3 it is almost the same (about 665 um), so low concentrations have little effect.
As the concentration rises to 10, 50 and 100 ug cm^-3 the length falls to about 600, 395 and 235 um.
At 200 ug cm^-3 the length is only about 62 um, so Verapamil inhibits pollen tube growth, and the higher the concentration the greater the inhibition (a negative correlation).
This fits calcium ions being needed for pollen tube growth, because Verapamil blocks calcium uptake.

questions.question: Explain why Verapamil, which blocks calcium ion uptake, can reduce the strength of cell walls.
questions.answer: Verapamil blocks Ca2+ uptake, so less calcium is available to cross-link pectin and strengthen the wall.
steps: Calcium ions bind to pectin in the cell wall, forming calcium pectate cross-links.
These cross-links hold the wall components together and give it strength.
Verapamil inhibits the uptake of calcium ions by the pollen tube.
With fewer calcium ions, fewer cross-links form, so the cell wall is weaker.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term species.
questions.answer: A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
steps: Members of a species are similar in structure and genetics.
They can breed with each other in nature.
Their offspring are fertile, so they can breed in turn.
Members are reproductively isolated from other species.

questions.question: Using the graph, explain the relationship between herbicide concentration and the mean number of insect species in three fields.
questions.answer: As herbicide concentration rises the mean number of insect species falls (negative relationship), from about 9 species with none to about 2.8 species at 100 mg dm^-3, because the herbicide removes the plants that insects depend on.
steps: The graph shows a negative relationship: the mean number of insect species falls from about 9 at 0 mg dm^-3 to about 6.2 at 20 and about 4 at 60, and to about 2.8 at 100 mg dm^-3 (a 69% decrease).
The fall is steepest at low concentrations (about 3 species lost by 20 mg dm^-3) and flattens at high concentrations.
Herbicide kills plants, so herbivorous insects lose their food source and habitat (shelter, egg-laying sites), and insects that feed on those insects (predators and parasites) also lose food.

The more herbicide, the more plant species are killed, so the more insect species decline or are lost; herbicide may also kill some insects directly, and species that depend on only one plant are lost first, so biodiversity falls.

questions.question: Give one example of molecular evidence used to support the three-domain system.
questions.answer: Base sequences of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) or DNA.
steps: Molecular evidence compares the chemical makeup of genetic material.
Base sequences of rRNA are the classic example used by Woese.
Comparing sequences shows how closely organisms are related.
Any one of these sequence comparisons gives the mark.

questions.question: Describe the role of the scientific community in evaluating the evidence for the three-domain system.
questions.answer: Scientists check, repeat and peer review the evidence before the classification is accepted.
steps: Other scientists check the data and methods for errors and bias.
Results are published and reviewed by peers before acceptance.
Other laboratories repeat the work to confirm the results are reproducible.
Only evidence that survives this process is used to support the system.

questions.question: Which box in each row of the table shows whether each feature is found in each of the three domains?
questions.answer: Absence of a nuclear envelope: Archaea and Bacteria only; presence of circular DNA: Archaea and Bacteria only; presence of a cell membrane: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya; presence of ribosomes: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
steps: Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotes, so they have no nucleus or nuclear envelope (Eukarya do), so tick the second box ("Archaea and Bacteria only") for the first row.
Prokaryotes have a circular chromosome, whereas eukaryotes have linear chromosomes in a nucleus, so tick "Archaea and Bacteria only" for circular DNA.
All cells have a cell surface membrane, so tick the last column ("Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya") for the third row.
All cells have ribosomes (70S in prokaryotes and 80S in eukaryotes) to make proteins, so tick the last column for the fourth row.

questions.question: Suggest three reasons why the Ulin tree (Eusideroxylon zwageri) is endangered.
questions.answer: Overharvesting for timber; habitat loss from deforestation; slow growth or low reproduction rate.
steps: The wood is valuable, so trees are overharvested for timber.
Forest is cleared for farming and development, so habitat is lost.
Trees grow and reproduce slowly, so populations recover slowly.
Small, fragmented populations are vulnerable to disease and chance events.

questions.question: Calculate the width of the phloem vessel along line XY in micrometres, in standard form.
steps: Measure the line XY in the photograph: about 43 mm on the printed page (154 px at 745 px per 210 mm); a ruler measurement of 43 mm to 44 mm is expected.
Actual width = image width / magnification = 43 mm / 200 = 0.215 mm.
Convert to micrometres: 0.215 mm x 1000 = 215 um to 217 um, which is 2.2 x 10^2 um in standard form (to 2 s.f.).

questions.question: Describe the role of phloem in a plant.
questions.answer: Phloem transports organic solutes such as sucrose from source to sink in both directions.
steps: Phloem is made of sieve tube elements and companion cells.
It carries sucrose made in photosynthesis (the source) to other parts of the plant.
Sinks such as roots, growing tips, fruits and stores receive these solutes.
Transport is in both directions and uses energy from companion cells.

questions.question: How many of these statements about mature sclerenchyma fibres are correct? They contain cellulose microfibrils; they contain pits; they contain cytoplasm. A none B one C two D three.
questions.answer: C two (cellulose microfibrils and pits are correct; cytoplasm is not).
steps: Sclerenchyma fibres have thick walls containing cellulose microfibrils, so statement one is correct.
Their walls have pits, so statement two is correct.
Mature sclerenchyma cells are dead and have no cytoplasm, so statement three is wrong.
Two statements are correct, so the answer is C.

questions.question: Give three differences between the distribution of phloem and xylem in a root compared with a stem.
questions.answer: In roots, xylem and phloem share a central core with phloem between xylem arms; in stems they are in separate bundles with phloem outside xylem.
steps: In a root, xylem and phloem are grouped together in a central core.
In a root, xylem forms a star shape in the centre with phloem between its arms.
In a stem, xylem and phloem are in separate vascular bundles arranged around the edge.
In a stem, phloem lies outside the xylem in each bundle rather than alternating with it.

questions.question: Explain how the reintroduction of beavers to Scotland changed biodiversity.
questions.answer: Dams create ponds and wetlands, which are new habitats, so more species can live there and biodiversity rises.
steps: Beavers cut trees and gnaw branches to build dams.
Dams flood land and create ponds and wetlands, which are new habitats.
These habitats allow more species of plants, insects, fish and birds to live there.
Tree felling opens the canopy and increases light, so species richness goes up.

questions.question: Discuss two proposed solutions to the low genetic diversity of the 11 beavers introduced from Norway, using the map of European beaver locations.
questions.answer: Both solutions can add new alleles, but more beavers from the same small Norwegian population adds little genetic diversity, whereas beavers from several different locations add more alleles and reduce inbreeding, with a higher risk of disease and unsuitable subspecies.
steps: Genetic diversity means the number of different alleles in the population; only 11 founders carry few alleles, so there is inbreeding, genetic drift and a smaller ability to adapt to disease or change.

Solution 1 (more beavers from Norway): the Norwegian population is easy and quick to use, is a similar climate to Scotland and the same population, so beavers are well adapted and the risk of disease is lower; but on the map Norway has only a few small patches of beavers, so these animals are closely related and add few new alleles.

Solution 2 (beavers from several locations): the map shows beavers in many places, such as Sweden, Finland, the Baltic states, Poland, Russia, Germany and France, so beavers from unrelated populations would add many different alleles, which would greatly increase genetic diversity and reduce inbreeding.

Disadvantages of solution 2: beavers from distant populations could be a different subspecies, could be adapted to different conditions or carry different diseases or parasites, are more difficult and more costly to transport and need more licences; some of the western populations are small and isolated, so they have little diversity themselves.

Overall: using several populations (especially the large Scandinavian and Baltic ones) is likely to be the better way to increase genetic diversity, if the beavers are healthy and the same subspecies; Norway alone is simpler but less effective.

questions.question: The frequency of the recessive homozygous genotype in a beaver population is 0.09 (q^2). Calculate the percentage of beavers homozygous for the dominant allele, using p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1.
steps: q^2 = 0.09, so q = square root of 0.09 = 0.3.
Homozygous dominant frequency = p^2 = 0.7 x 0.7 = 0.49.
So 49 % of beavers are homozygous dominant; check: 0.49 + 0.42 + 0.09 = 1.

questions.question: Which term describes a frog found only in Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama? A diversity B endemic C polygenic D specific.
questions.answer: B endemic
steps: Endemic means found naturally in only one place or region.
Diversity refers to variety of species, not where they live.
Polygenic means controlled by many genes, which is not about location.
Specific does not describe a restricted geographic range, so the answer is B.

questions.question: Complete the table to show the type of each of the frog's three adaptations.
questions.answer: Bright red skin with black spots: anatomical (warning colouration); production of poison: physiological (biochemical); adhesive discs on toes: anatomical.
steps: Adaptations can be anatomical (structural), physiological (processes inside the body) or behavioural (how the animal acts).
The bright red skin with black spots and the adhesive discs on the toes are structural features, so they are anatomical.
Making a poison is a biochemical process in the cells, so it is physiological.

questions.question: Suggest the advantages to the frog of its bright skin, paralysis-causing poison and adhesive toe discs.
questions.answer: Bright skin warns predators and the poison deters them; sticky discs help it climb and escape.
steps: Bright red skin with black spots is a warning colour that predators learn to avoid.
The powerful poison paralyses or deters predators, so the frog is less likely to be eaten.
Adhesive discs let the frog grip leaves and climb.
Climbing helps it reach food and escape from ground predators.

questions.question: Suggest how natural selection could have given rise to frogs that produce poison.
questions.answer: Random mutation gave some frogs poison production; poisonous frogs survived and bred more, so the allele became more common.
steps: Random mutations create variation in the ability to produce poison.
Frogs with poison are less likely to be eaten by predators.
They survive longer and produce more offspring, passing on the allele.
Over many generations the allele for poison production increases in frequency.

questions.question: Which can be used to calculate genetic diversity? A Hardy-Weinberg equation B heterozygosity index C index of diversity D mitotic index.
questions.answer: B heterozygosity index
steps: Genetic diversity means variety of alleles within a species.
The heterozygosity index measures how many individuals are heterozygous, which reflects allele variety.
The index of diversity measures species diversity, not genetic diversity.
The mitotic index measures cell division, and the Hardy-Weinberg equation predicts allele frequencies.

questions.question: Give two differences between genetic diversity and species richness.
questions.answer: Genetic diversity is variety of alleles within a species; species richness is the number of different species in an area.
steps: Genetic diversity concerns variation in alleles within one species.
Species richness counts the number of different species in an area.
Genetic diversity is measured using heterozygosity; species richness is measured by counting species.
Genetic diversity is within-species variety, while species richness is between-species variety.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons why seed banks store seeds instead of growing whole plants.
questions.answer: Seeds take up much less space and need less maintenance; they can stay viable for long periods.
steps: Seeds are small, so many varieties need much less storage space than whole plants.
Seeds are dormant, so they need little food, water or care.
Seeds can stay viable for many years when dried and kept cold.
Growing whole plants would be costly and would need land and labour.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage increase in the mass of bananas imported by one country from 2007 to 2011, using the table.
steps: China imported 3.3 x 10^5 tonnes in 2007 and 8.2 x 10^5 tonnes in 2011.
Increase = 8.2 - 3.3 = 4.9 x 10^5 tonnes.
Percentage increase = 4.9 / 3.3 x 100 = 148.5%.

questions.question: Explain why scientists are breeding the Cavendish banana with other banana varieties, given that Cavendish clones are not resistant to Panama disease.
questions.answer: Cavendish clones are genetically identical and not resistant; other varieties may carry resistance alleles that breeding can bring in.
steps: Cavendish bananas are clones, so they all have the same alleles and little genetic diversity.
They are not resistant to the Panama disease fungus, which can destroy whole plantations.
Other varieties may carry alleles that confer resistance to the fungus.
Breeding combines these alleles, so some offspring may be resistant while keeping good crop traits.

questions.question: Give one reason why the cells were stained with acetic orcein in this investigation.
questions.answer: To make the chromosomes (nuclei) visible so that dividing cells can be seen under the microscope.
steps: Unstained cells are almost transparent under a light microscope.
Acetic orcein binds to chromatin/DNA and stains chromosomes dark.
Stained chromosomes can be seen clearly and their stage identified.
Being able to see dividing cells is needed to count the mitotic index.

questions.question: Which labelled cell (P, Q, R or S) in the photograph is in metaphase of mitosis?
questions.answer: C: R
steps: In metaphase the chromosomes are condensed and lined up at the equator (centre) of the cell, attached to spindle fibres.
Cell R has its chromosomes arranged across the middle of the cell, so it is in metaphase.

Q has coiled, condensed chromosomes spread through the nucleus area (prophase), S has chromatids being pulled to two poles (anaphase) and P has two separate groups of chromosomes at opposite ends with a cell plate forming (telophase).

questions.question: Using the table of results, calculate the mitotic index of the tendril tip cells.
steps: Mitotic index = number of cells in mitosis / total number of cells.
Cells in mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase) = 15 + 3 + 10 + 5 = 33.
Total cells = 117 + 33 = 150, so mitotic index = 33 / 150 = 0.22 (22%).

questions.question: Suggest the advantages of tendrils to the pea plant.
questions.answer: Tendrils let the plant climb to reach light for photosynthesis and save energy on stem support.
steps: Tendrils coil around supports, so the plant can climb.
Climbing lifts leaves into light, improving photosynthesis.
The plant does not need to make thick, strong stem tissue, saving energy.
Climbing also helps the plant spread over other plants and reach more area.

questions.question: Explain how the separation of chromosomes in meiosis gives rise to genetic variation in pea plant offspring.
questions.answer: Independent assortment of homologous chromosomes and crossing over make different allele combinations in gametes.
steps: In metaphase I homologous pairs line up randomly, so maternal and paternal chromosomes are mixed.
This independent assortment gives gametes with different combinations of alleles.
Crossing over in prophase I swaps alleles between non-sister chromatids.
Random fusion of gametes at fertilisation adds further variation.

questions.question: Describe two anatomical adaptations of the Tristan albatross that enable it to occupy its niche.
questions.answer: Long narrow wings for soaring over the ocean; webbed feet for swimming; hooked bill for catching fish and squid.
steps: Long, narrow wings allow efficient gliding and soaring over long distances.
Webbed feet help the bird swim and paddle on the sea surface.
A hooked bill grips slippery fish, octopus and squid.
Waterproof plumage helps the bird stay buoyant and warm at sea.

questions.question: The Tristan albatross population is 4500 and is predicted to decline by 5.3 % per year. Calculate the predicted population after one year.
steps: A 5.3 % decline leaves 100 - 5.3 = 94.7 % of the population.
Rounded to a whole number, the population is about 4262 birds.
The population is predicted to fall by about 238 birds in one year.

questions.question: Suggest why the Tristan albatross and wandering albatross were once classified as the same species.
questions.answer: They look very similar in appearance (similar morphology).
steps: Classification was originally based on physical appearance (morphology).
The two albatrosses share many similar physical features.
Similar appearance led scientists to group them as one species.
Later genetic evidence showed they are separate species.

questions.question: Suggest how the mice on the island evolved into a new species, given they are now 50 % larger than normal mice.
questions.answer: Mutations gave variation in size; larger mice survived and bred, and isolation stopped gene flow until they became a new species.
steps: Random mutations produce variation in body size among island mice.
Larger mice can eat and survive better, so they are more likely to breed.
The island isolates them from mainland mice, so no gene flow occurs.
Over many generations differences accumulate until they cannot interbreed with the original population.

questions.question: Explain how the critically endangered Tristan albatross could be conserved, using the information in the question, including strategies on the island and involving zoos in other countries.
questions.answer: Control the mice on the island to protect chicks, and use zoos abroad for captive breeding and later reintroduction.
steps: Mice prey on albatross chicks, so reducing mouse numbers on the island protects chicks.
Predator-proof fencing or trapping of mice on nesting areas also helps chick survival.
Monitoring the wild population shows whether the strategies are working.
Zoos in other countries can breed birds in captivity, increasing numbers.
Captive breeding can maintain genetic diversity through managed pairings.
Birds bred in zoos can later be reintroduced to the wild to rebuild the population.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term endemic with reference to the Madagascan pygmy kingfisher.
questions.answer: It is found naturally only in Madagascar (in its forests) and nowhere else in the world.
steps: Endemic means a species is restricted to one geographic area.
The Madagascan pygmy kingfisher is found only in Madagascar's forests.
It is not found naturally anywhere else.
So it is endemic to Madagascar.

questions.question: State the domain in which this kingfisher is classified.
questions.answer: Eukarya.
steps: The kingfisher is a multicellular animal.
Animal cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Organisms with eukaryotic cells belong to the Eukarya domain.
So the domain is Eukarya.

questions.question: Using the proposed reclassification diagram, explain which kingfisher species are most closely related to Ceyx madagascariensis.
questions.answer: Alcedo leucogaster and Alcedo cristata are the most closely related to Ceyx madagascariensis, because they share the most recent common ancestor with it on the proposed tree.
steps: In the proposed reclassification, C. madagascariensis branches from the same node as the two Alcedo species (A. leucogaster and A. cristata).
Species sharing the most recent (nearest) common ancestor are the most closely related, so the two Alcedo species are its closest relatives.
Ceyx lecontei and Ceyx picta branch off earlier, so they are less closely related, even though they share the genus name Ceyx.

questions.question: Explain how molecular evidence led to the reclassification of kingfisher species and how the scientific community would have reviewed the evidence before it was accepted.
questions.answer: DNA base sequences showed relationships; the new data were then published and peer reviewed and repeated before acceptance.
steps: Scientists sequenced DNA or other genetic material from the kingfisher species.
Comparing base sequences showed which species are most closely related.
The results conflicted with the old morphology-based classification, so species were moved.
The new data were submitted for publication and checked by other scientists (peer review).
Other laboratories repeated the analysis to confirm the results are reproducible.
Only once the evidence was checked and accepted was the reclassification adopted.

questions.question: Which describes species richness in Bhitarkanika National Park? A the number of animal species B the number of plant species C the number of organisms in each of the species D the number of species.
questions.answer: D the number of species
steps: Species richness is the number of different species in an area.
Option A counts only animal species, which is too narrow.
Option B counts only plant species, which is too narrow.
Option C counts individuals, not species, so the answer is D.

questions.question: Describe one other way the biodiversity of the Bhitarkanika area could be measured.
questions.answer: Calculate the index of diversity using the number of individuals of each species.
steps: Count the number of individuals of each species in a sample.
Find the total number of individuals, N.
Use D = N(N-1) / sum of n(n-1) for each species n.
A higher D means greater biodiversity.

questions.question: Explain the possible causes of the decrease in the endangered saltwater crocodile population over the past 40 years.
questions.answer: Hunting for skins and meat, loss of river and mangrove habitat, and pollution.
steps: Crocodiles are hunted for their skins and meat, reducing adult numbers.
Habitat such as mangroves and rivers is cleared for farming and development.
Pollution of the rivers harms crocodiles and their prey.
Human-crocodile conflict can lead to animals being killed.

questions.question: Using the graph of temperature against percentage of male hatchlings, calculate the number of female crocodiles from 350 eggs incubated at 32 deg C.
questions.answer: About 270 females (269.5)
steps: From the graph, at 32 degrees C about 23% of the crocodiles hatch as male.
So the percentage female = 100 - 23 = 77%.
Number of females = 350 x 77 / 100 = 269.5, about 270 females.

questions.question: Explain how the egg collection and incubation project could increase crocodile numbers rapidly without reducing future genetic diversity, using the graph.
questions.answer: Collecting eggs from many nests and incubating them protects them, so more hatch and numbers rise quickly; choosing temperatures that give mostly females increases breeding output, while still producing enough males from many different parents keeps genetic diversity.
steps: Eggs collected from nests in different parts of the park come from many different parents, so the hatchlings carry many different alleles and the genetic diversity of the future population is kept.

Incubating the eggs at a suitable temperature (and releasing them after hatching) protects them from predators, flooding and unsuitable temperatures, so a higher percentage hatch and the population increases quickly.

The graph shows temperature determines sex: at 28 degrees C 0% are male, at 29 degrees C about 6%, at 30 degrees C about 40%, at 31 degrees C about 82% (the maximum) and at 32 to 33 degrees C only about 23% and 21%; so the sex ratio can be controlled.
Incubating at a temperature such as 29 to 30 degrees C gives more females (60 to 94%), and each female lays many eggs, so the population grows faster than with mostly males (31 degrees C).

But some males must also be produced (not 28 degrees C, which gives none), from many different nests, so that the females can mate with many different males and the genetic diversity is not reduced by inbreeding.

questions.question: The urban population of Santa Cruz was 17 000 in 2020 and makes up 85 % of the total. The population grows by 6.4 % per year. Predict the total population in 2025.
questions.answer: About 27 273 people.
steps: Total population in 2020 = 17 000 / 0.85 = 20 000.
Growth factor per year = 1.064.
From 2020 to 2025 is 5 years, so population = 20 000 x 1.064^5.

questions.question: Using the graph of tourist numbers and recorded non-endemic species, state the relationship shown.
questions.answer: Positive correlation: as the number of tourists increases, the number of recorded non-endemic species increases.
steps: The points rise from about 480 non-endemic species at about 17 000 tourists to about 1 530 species at about 225 000 tourists.
So there is a positive correlation (the rise is quicker at low tourist numbers and slows at high numbers), but correlation does not prove that tourists cause the introduction of species.

questions.question: Using the table of species counts from the native forest in 1960, calculate the index of diversity (D) to one decimal place.
steps: Total number of individuals N = 21 + 2 + 4 + 13 + 54 + 15 + 6 + 32 = 147.
Fill in the missing values of n(n - 1): 420, 156, 2862 and 992, so the sum of n(n - 1) = 420 + 2 + 12 + 156 + 2862 + 210 + 30 + 992 = 4684.
D = N(N - 1) / sum of n(n - 1) = 147 x 146 / 4684 = 21 462 / 4684 = 4.58, which is 4.6 to one decimal place.

questions.question: Explain why the spread of the wild blackberry affects the biodiversity of Santa Cruz.
questions.answer: The blackberry outcompetes native endemic plants for light, space and water, so native species and their habitats are lost and diversity falls.
steps: The wild blackberry grows fast and forms dense thickets across the island.
It outcompetes native plants for light, water, minerals and space.
Native endemic plants decline or disappear from the forest.
Animals that depend on native plants for food and shelter lose their habitat and decline.
The loss of species reduces species richness and possibly genetic diversity of the island.

questions.question: Explain how cortical granules ensure that the egg cell is diploid after fertilisation.
questions.answer: Cortical granules harden the zona pellucida to block polyspermy, so only one haploid sperm fuses with the haploid egg.
steps: Cortical granules are released from the egg after the first sperm enters.
They release enzymes that harden the zona pellucida around the egg.
The hardened layer blocks other sperm from entering (blocks polyspermy).
Only one haploid sperm nucleus fuses with the haploid egg nucleus, giving a diploid zygote.

questions.question: Comment on the effect of three mating strategies (sperm middle region length, spermatophores, sperm storage) on reproductive success and offspring genetic diversity, using the graph and diagram.
questions.answer: A longer middle region gives faster sperm (positive correlation), so those males fertilise more eggs; spermatophores raise a male's success but reduce female mating variety; sperm storage lets females have offspring from several males and so increases genetic diversity.
steps: Middle region: the graph shows a positive correlation, as the length of the middle region increases from about 15 to 19 um the swimming speed increases from about 45 to 75 um s^-1; the middle region contains the mitochondria, so a longer one gives more ATP and faster swimming.

Since females mate with many males, sperm from different males compete, and faster sperm are more likely to reach and fertilise the egg first, so males with a longer middle region have greater reproductive success (and pass on the allele for a long middle region).

Spermatophores: nutrients help the female make more or better eggs, so both parents gain, and the chemicals make her less attractive to other males, so the male is more likely to be the father of all her offspring (greater male reproductive success); but the female mates with fewer males, so the genetic diversity of her offspring is lower.

Sperm storage (turtles): the female can fertilise eggs in years with no mating, and her offspring can have different fathers (stored sperm from numerous males), so her reproductive success and the genetic diversity of the offspring are higher; a male's success is less certain because his sperm competes with sperm from other males.

Overall these strategies increase the reproductive success of the individual using them (males with fast sperm or spermatophores, females with stored sperm), but those that limit female mating reduce genetic variation.

questions.question: Calculate the magnification of the photograph of M. smithii, to two significant figures.
steps: Magnification = length of the scale bar in the image / actual length it represents.
The 1200 nm scale bar measures about 40 mm on the printed page (about 142 px at 745 px per 210 mm); a ruler should give 39 mm to 41 mm.
Convert: 40 mm = 4.0 x 10^7 nm, so magnification = 4.0 x 10^7 / 1200 = 33 000 = 3.3 x 10^4 (to 2 significant figures).

questions.question: Explain which type of microscope was used to take the photograph of M. smithii.
questions.answer: A scanning electron microscope (SEM).
steps: The image shows the three-dimensional surface of the cells with shading, which is what a scanning electron microscope produces (a transmission electron microscope gives a flat 2D slice showing the inside of the cell).

A light microscope could not be used because the cells are only about 1 um across (the 1200 nm scale bar is about the width of a cell), which is close to the resolution limit of about 200 nm, and the magnification is about 30 000, which a light microscope cannot reach.

questions.question: Describe the information scientists would have used to classify M. smithii into the Archaea domain.
questions.answer: Ribosomal RNA or DNA base sequences, plus prokaryotic features such as no nucleus and distinctive archaeal membrane lipids and cell wall.
steps: Scientists compared the rRNA or DNA base sequences with those of known Archaea.
Similar sequences place M. smithii in the Archaea lineage.
Its cells are prokaryotic, with no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles.
Its membrane lipids and cell wall differ from Bacteria, supporting the Archaea classification.

questions.question: Explain how scientists could confirm that M. smithii and M. oralis are different species of Archaea.
questions.answer: Compare their DNA or rRNA base sequences; a large enough difference shows they are different species.
steps: Sequence the DNA or rRNA of both microorganisms.
Compare the base sequences and count the differences.
A large number of differences shows the two are genetically distinct.
Distinct sequences, and no successful exchange of genes, confirm they are different species.

questions.question: Describe the effect of length of storage time on the germination of the stored seeds, using the graph.
questions.answer: The percentage of seeds that germinate stays high at first, then falls steeply as storage time increases, then levels off at a very low percentage.
steps: At first the percentage of seeds that germinate stays at a high constant value (a plateau) for the early period of storage.
Then the percentage falls rapidly, so the longer the seeds are stored, the fewer germinate.
The fall then levels off near 0%, so after a long time almost no seeds germinate.

questions.question: Explain the advantages of storing seeds from many plants of one species and regularly germinating samples of the stored seeds.
questions.answer: Many plants preserve genetic diversity and reduce inbreeding; germinating samples checks viability and replenishes stocks.
steps: Seeds from many plants give a wider range of alleles, maintaining genetic diversity.
A wider gene pool reduces the risk of inbreeding and of losing the species to one disease.
Regularly germinating samples tests whether stored seeds are still viable.
Growing plants from samples produces fresh seeds to replace the stored stock.

questions.question: A company produces 130 000 kg of bioplastic cutlery and straws per month; 40 % are straws. Calculate the mass of cutlery produced per year to two significant figures.
questions.answer: 9.4 x 10^5 kg (936 000 kg per year).
steps: Cutlery is 100 % - 40 % = 60 % of the product.
Cutlery per month = 0.60 x 130 000 = 78 000 kg.
Cutlery per year = 78 000 x 12 = 936 000 kg.
To two significant figures this is 9.4 x 10^5 kg.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the term sustainable with reference to cutlery made from avocado seeds.
questions.answer: It meets present needs from a renewable resource (avocado seeds) without depleting resources for future generations.
steps: Avocado seeds are a by-product of food production, so they are renewable.
Using them does not use up finite oil reserves like oil-based plastic.
Plant-based cutlery can biodegrade, reducing long-term pollution.
So the product meets present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

questions.question: Complete the table showing the type of each adaptation shown by this caterpillar.
questions.answer: Looks like a pit viper snake: anatomical; tries to strike potential predators: behavioural.
steps: Looking like a snake is a structural feature of the body (shape, colour and markings, a form of mimicry), so it is an anatomical adaptation.
Striking at predators is the way the animal acts, so it is a behavioural adaptation.

questions.question: State the type of microscope used to view the organelle shown in the photograph.
questions.answer: A transmission electron microscope (TEM).
steps: The photograph shows internal membranes (cristae) of a mitochondrion in a thin slice at a magnification of x72 500, which is far beyond a light microscope.
A flat, internal 2D view of the organelle is typical of a transmission electron microscope.

questions.question: Describe the function of the organelle shown in the photograph.
questions.answer: The organelle is a mitochondrion: it carries out aerobic respiration, which makes ATP for the cell.
steps: The structure has a double membrane, with the inner membrane folded into cristae, so it is a mitochondrion.
It is the site of aerobic respiration: the Krebs cycle takes place in the matrix and the electron transport chain (oxidative phosphorylation) on the cristae, making most of the cell's ATP.
ATP is the energy source for cell processes such as active transport, protein synthesis and movement, and the cristae give a large surface area for ATP synthesis.

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of rough endoplasmic reticulum.
questions.answer: Draw a stack of flattened membrane-bound sacs (cisternae) with small dots (ribosomes) on the outer surface, connected to the nuclear envelope; label rough endoplasmic reticulum, cisterna (lumen), membrane and ribosomes.
steps: Draw 3 to 5 long, flattened, parallel sacs (cisternae) formed by a membrane, close together and joined at the ends or folded, and labelled "cisternae" or "lumen".
Draw many small dots on the outside surface of the membrane and label them "ribosomes" (this is what makes the ER rough).
Show it connected to the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope, if space allows, and label with label lines "rough endoplasmic reticulum".

questions.question: Sketch a graph showing the distribution of a phenotype with continuous variation in a population.
questions.answer: A symmetrical bell-shaped (normal distribution) curve, with the phenotype (e.g. height or mass) on the x axis and the number of individuals (frequency) on the y axis, peaking at the mean.
steps: Label the axes: x axis = the measured phenotype (e.g. height / cm, a continuous variable) and y axis = number of individuals (frequency).
Draw a smooth, symmetrical bell-shaped curve with the highest point (the mean) in the middle and the curve tailing off to the left and right without touching the axis.
Continuous variation (a range with no clear categories, caused by many genes and the environment) therefore gives a normal distribution.

questions.question: Explain how a mutation could cause a chicken embryo to develop teeth, given the tooth genes are normally switched off.
questions.answer: A mutation in the regulatory (switch) region turns the tooth genes on, so they are transcribed and translated into proteins that form teeth.
steps: Chicken genomes already contain the genes for tooth production.
A mutation in the promoter or other regulatory region can stop the repression that switches the gene off.
The tooth gene is then transcribed to mRNA.
The mRNA is translated into proteins that direct tooth development in the embryo.

questions.question: In a goat population there are 470 brown goats and 140 white goats (white is bb). Calculate the frequency of allele B to two decimal places.
steps: Total goats = 470 + 140 = 610.
White goats are bb, so q^2 = 140 / 610 = 0.2295.
q = square root of 0.2295 = 0.479.
p = 1 - q = 0.521, so the frequency of allele B is 0.52.

questions.question: Name the organelles containing starch granules in cassava root cells.
questions.answer: Amyloplasts.
steps: Amyloplasts are plastids that store starch.
They are found in storage tissues such as cassava roots.
They contain starch granules, as shown in the micrograph.
So the organelles are amyloplasts.

questions.question: Explain how the structure of starch relates to its function.
questions.answer: Starch is insoluble and compact, so it stores glucose without affecting water potential; its branched structure allows fast hydrolysis.
steps: Starch is insoluble, so it does not change the water potential of the cell.
Its coiled, compact helix stores many glucose units in a small space.
Branched amylopectin has many ends, so enzymes can release glucose quickly.
Glucose from starch hydrolysis is then used in respiration to release energy.

questions.question: Using the graph, which percentage of the world cassava crop is grown in Africa? A 33 % B 34 % C 66 % D 67 %.
steps: Read the cassava bars: African production is about 160 million tonnes per year and world production about 240 million tonnes per year.
Percentage = 160 / 240 x 100 = 66.7%, which is 67%, so D.

questions.question: Calculate the predicted world maize production after a 2.3 % increase, to the nearest whole number.
questions.answer: 1074 million tonnes
steps: Read the world maize bar: about 1050 million tonnes per year.
To the nearest whole number: 1074 million tonnes.

questions.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of growing three crop plants for human food, using the cassava graph and table.
questions.answer: Cassava needs little water and few nutrients and gives a lot of carbohydrate, but bitter cassava is toxic and all cassava is low in protein; maize has more protein and few toxins but needs more water and nutrients and has less carbohydrate.
steps: Advantages of cassava: low to medium water need and low nutrient need, so it grows in poor soil and dry areas; carbohydrate content is about 95 g per 100 g dry mass compared with 77 g for maize.
Bitter cassava gives a higher yield (mean dry mass about 0.23 kg per plant against about 0.16 kg for sweet cassava) and its bitter chemicals protect it against animals.

Disadvantages: the bitter chemicals (100 to 500 mg kg^-1 in bitter, 10 to 50 in sweet, 1 to 2 in maize) release hydrogen cyanide, which stops respiration, so the cassava must be processed before eating.
Cassava has very little protein (about 1.8 g per 100 g against 8.75 g in maize), so a diet based on it could lead to protein deficiency.

Maize is a good source of protein and has little toxin, but it needs medium to high water and nutrients (irrigation and fertiliser) and gives less carbohydrate; sweet cassava is safer than bitter but gives a lower yield.

questions.question: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube of length 2.5 cm.
steps: Surface area = 6 x 2.5^2 = 37.5 cm^2.
So the surface area : volume ratio is 2.4 : 1.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term habitat.
questions.answer: The place or environment where an organism lives.
steps: A habitat is the place where an organism normally lives.
It provides the food, shelter and conditions the organism needs.
Habitats can be large (a forest) or small (a pond).
It is the environment in which the organism lives.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term species.
questions.answer: A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
steps: Members of a species are similar in structure and genetics.
They can interbreed in nature.
Their offspring are fertile, so the species is reproductively isolated.
This separates them from other species.

questions.question: State what is meant by polygenic inheritance with reference to wombat height.
questions.answer: Height is controlled by many genes at different loci, each with a small additive effect, giving continuous variation.
steps: Polygenic means many genes control one characteristic.
Each gene at a different locus adds a small amount to height.
The combined effect of all alleles produces a range of heights.
This gives continuous variation rather than a few distinct classes.

questions.question: Describe two anatomical adaptations of the common wombat that help it dig burrows.
questions.answer: Strong, sharp claws for digging; short, powerful limbs for pushing soil.
steps: Strong, sharp claws on the forefeet break up and loosen soil.
Short, powerful limbs generate force to dig and push soil out.
A broad, robust body and skeleton support digging forces.
These features suit a burrowing animal living in a burrow.

questions.question: Suggest how human activity could have caused the extinction of the Sehuencas water frog in the wild.
questions.answer: Habitat destruction and water pollution reduce the frog's habitat, and introduced species or overhunting cut numbers further.
steps: Clearing forest for farming or building destroys the frog's habitat.
Pollution of streams and water harms the frog's eggs and tadpoles.
Introduced species may prey on frogs or compete with them.
Smaller, fragmented populations become too few to survive and breed.

questions.question: Explain how resistance to the fungal disease could develop in a population of Sehuencas water frogs.
questions.answer: A mutation gives some frogs resistance; resistant frogs survive and breed, so the resistance allele becomes more common by natural selection.
steps: A random mutation produces an allele that confers resistance to the fungus.
Frogs with this allele survive infection while others die.
Surviving resistant frogs breed and pass on the resistance allele.
Over generations the allele frequency increases in the population.

questions.question: Describe how the scientists could calculate the heterozygosity index for a population of Sehuencas water frogs.
questions.answer: Sample individuals, count those that are heterozygous at a gene, and divide by the total number sampled.
steps: Sample a set of frogs from the population.
Test each frog's genotype at a given gene to find heterozygotes.
Count the number of heterozygous individuals.
Divide the number of heterozygotes by the total number of frogs sampled.

questions.question: Describe the role of zoos in the conservation of endangered Sehuencas water frogs.
questions.answer: Zoos hold a captive breeding programme to increase numbers, manage genetic diversity, support reintroduction and research disease.
steps: Zoos keep a captive population, which can grow when wild numbers are very low.
Breeding is managed using a studbook to avoid inbreeding and keep genetic diversity.
Captive-bred frogs can be reintroduced to suitable wild habitats.
Zoos can research the fungal disease and how to treat or prevent it.
Zoos can store gametes or samples as a backup genetic resource.
Zoos educate the public and raise funds to protect the frog's habitat.

questions.question: Which term describes a tortoise found only on the Galapagos Islands? A diversity B endemic C isolation D linkage.
questions.answer: B endemic
steps: Endemic means found naturally in only one place.
Diversity refers to the variety of species, not location.
Isolation describes separation of populations, not a species' range.
Linkage refers to genes on the same chromosome, so the answer is B.

questions.question: Complete the table showing the type of each of the tortoise's adaptations (long neck, arched shell).
questions.answer: Long neck: anatomical; shell that arches above neck: anatomical; making themselves look as large as possible: behavioural.
steps: A long neck and a raised shell are structural features of the body, so they are anatomical adaptations.
Making themselves look big during a dispute is something the animal does (stretching the neck and raising the body), so it is a behavioural adaptation.

questions.question: Suggest one selection pressure that has resulted in the development of one of these features.
questions.answer: Competition between males for territory and mates (sexual selection).
steps: Tortoises fight over territory and mates.
Males that look larger win more disputes and mating opportunities.
Those with longer necks and arched shells therefore survive and breed more.
Over time the features become more common.

questions.question: Using the diagram of offspring and fathers, calculate the percentage of female 10's offspring that were fathered by male B.
steps: Female 10 has 27 offspring in total (the height of the bar).
Father A (dark part) fathered 9 of them, and father B (grey part) fathered the rest, 27 - 9 = 18 (there is no part for male C).
Percentage fathered by B = 18 / 27 x 100 = 66.7%.

questions.question: The wild population of C. hoodensis is now 1800; in 1963 there were 15 in the wild. Calculate the percentage increase, to one decimal place.
questions.answer: 11 900.0 % increase (119-fold).
steps: Wild population in 1963 = 3 males + 12 females = 15.
Percentage increase = 1785 / 15 x 100 = 11 900.0 %.
This assumes 15 was the whole wild population in 1963.

questions.question: Explain how the zoo could determine that its captive-bred giant tortoise was a C. hoodensis tortoise.
questions.answer: Compare the tortoise's DNA base sequences with reference DNA from known C. hoodensis; matching sequences confirm the species.
steps: Take a DNA sample from the zoo tortoise.
Sequence a gene or marker region and compare it with reference C. hoodensis sequences.
Very similar sequences show that the tortoise is the same species.
Differences from other species' sequences confirm it is not a different tortoise species.

questions.question: Explain how a change in frequency of a recessive allele in the tortoise population could be determined.
questions.answer: Count recessive homozygotes at different times, calculate q from q^2, and compare q values over time.
steps: Sample the population at different times and count recessive phenotype individuals.
Their frequency gives q^2, so q is the square root of this value.
Calculate q for each sample.
A change in q between samples shows the allele frequency is changing.

questions.question: Explain why the percentage of young tree shoots eaten by elk changed after the introduction of wolves.
questions.answer: Wolves reduce elk numbers and make elk avoid open riverside areas, so fewer young shoots are eaten.
steps: Wolves are predators of elk, so elk numbers fall.
Elk become wary and avoid feeding in open habitats where wolves can hunt them.
With fewer elk and less time in risky areas, fewer young shoots are browsed.
Young trees can grow taller, increasing the percentage of shoots surviving.

questions.question: Using the graph, describe the relationship between elk density and mean beaver lifespan.
questions.answer: There is a negative relationship: as the number of elk per km^2 increases, the mean beaver lifespan falls, steeply from 30 to 60 elk km^-2, and levels off at about 20 years above 80 elk km^-2.
steps: Negative correlation: the mean beaver lifespan is highest (about 76 years) at the lowest elk density shown (30 elk per km^2) and falls as the number of elk rises.
The fall is steep at first (about 76 at 30, 45 at 40, 37 at 50 and 28 at 60 elk per km^2), and then more gradual (22 at 70 elk per km^2).
Above about 80 elk per km^2 the lifespan stays constant at about 20 years, so more elk beyond this density has no further effect.

questions.question: Suggest what information scientists would need to collect to calculate species richness in a habitat in Yellowstone National Park.
questions.answer: The number of different species present in the habitat, found by surveying and identifying all species in sample areas.
steps: Survey the habitat using standard sampling methods such as quadrats or transects.
Identify every species present in the sample areas.
Count the number of different species recorded.
Repeat across the habitat to make sure the count represents the whole area.

questions.question: Write a formula that could be used to determine the biodiversity of a habitat in Yellowstone National Park.
questions.answer: D = N(N-1) / sum of n(n-1), where N is the total number of individuals and n is the number of each species.
steps: N is the total number of individuals of all species.
n is the number of individuals of each species.
Sum the value of n(n-1) for every species.
Divide N(N-1) by this sum to give D.

questions.question: Discuss the effect of the introduction of wolves on the biodiversity of Yellowstone, using all the information in the question and its graphs.
questions.answer: Wolves reduced the number of elk, so young shoots survived and grew into trees, which supported more beaver colonies that created ponds; so biodiversity increased (a trophic cascade).
steps: After wolves (predators of elk) were introduced in 1995, the number of wolves rose to about 100 (2003) and the number of elk fell from about 17 000 to about 6 000, and the percentage of young shoots eaten fell from 100% to 19% in the forest and 2% in the riverside habitat.

With less grazing, young cottonwood shoots over 5 cm tall rose from 0 (before 2004) to about 160 in 2010, so more trees grew, giving more food, shelter and nesting sites for other organisms (birds and insects) and stabilising the river banks.
Beavers use trees to build dams, and the number of beaver colonies rose from about 1 (to 1999) to about 12 in 2009; beaver lifespan is longer when elk density is lower, which also helps.

Beaver dams create new habitats such as ponds, which support more species (fish, amphibians, invertebrates, water birds), and wolf kills feed scavengers, so overall the species richness and biodiversity increase.

The wolves act as a keystone predator, so the effects pass through the food web; but the data show correlations only, there are time lags (cottonwood after 2003), and other factors such as climate or hunting may also contribute.

questions.question: The body cells of a female Indian muntjac have three pairs of chromosomes. Dividing cells can be taken from the body of a female Indian muntjac. Draw one of these body cells showing the arrangement of chromosomes in the anaphase stage of mitosis.
questions.answer: Draw a cell with a spindle and 6 V-shaped chromosomes at each pole (12 in all), with the centromeres nearest the poles and the arms trailing towards the equator.
steps: The female Indian muntjac has 3 pairs (6 chromosomes), so after DNA replication it has 6 chromosomes, each of 2 chromatids.
In anaphase the centromeres divide and the sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles, so draw 6 single chromatids moving to each end of the cell (12 in total).

Draw each chromatid as a V (or J) shape with the centromere leading towards the pole, spindle fibres from the poles to the centromeres, and a cell outline (with no nucleus visible and the cell perhaps starting to elongate).

questions.question: Calculate the angle representing anaphase on the pie chart, given interphase lasts 9 hours and anaphase 20 minutes.
questions.answer: 10 degrees
steps: Interphase takes 9 hours and is shown as 270 degrees on the pie chart, so 1 hour is 30 degrees.
Anaphase lasts 20 minutes = 1/3 hour.
Angle = 1/3 x 30 = 10 degrees.

questions.question: The diagram shows one of the chromosomes in an Indian muntjac cell. State what is meant by the term locus.
questions.answer: The position of a gene on a chromosome.
steps: A locus is a fixed position on a chromosome.
Each gene occupies a particular locus.
Alleles of the same gene occupy the same locus on homologous chromosomes.
So the locus is the gene's position on a chromosome.

questions.question: Explain how the chromosomes of an Indian muntjac egg cell could differ from those in a body cell.
questions.answer: The egg is haploid, with one chromosome from each pair, and its chromosomes are a mix of maternal and paternal alleles from meiosis.
steps: Body cells are diploid, with three pairs of homologous chromosomes.
The egg cell is formed by meiosis, so it has only three chromosomes, one from each pair.
Independent assortment and crossing over mix maternal and paternal alleles.
So the egg chromosomes carry different allele combinations from body cell chromosomes.

questions.question: Chinese muntjac cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes. The Chinese muntjac looks similar to the Indian muntjac (which has three pairs), but if they breed together they produce offspring that are infertile. Suggest why the offspring would be infertile.
questions.answer: Their chromosome numbers differ, so homologous chromosomes cannot pair in meiosis and functional gametes cannot form.
steps: Chinese muntjacs have 23 pairs of chromosomes; Indian muntjacs have three pairs.
In the hybrid offspring, chromosomes from the two species do not match in pairs.
Chromosomes cannot pair correctly during meiosis.
Meiosis fails, so no fertile gametes are produced.

questions.question: Complete the plant cell diagram by drawing and labelling an amyloplast, a chloroplast and the tonoplast.
questions.answer: Draw a small oval chloroplast near the cell wall, a similar-sized amyloplast (with starch granules) near the wall, and a large vacuole in the centre with a line around it (the tonoplast); label all three.
steps: Tonoplast: draw a large rounded outline taking up most of the middle of the cell (the permanent vacuole) and label the line around it as tonoplast (the single membrane around the vacuole), leaving a thin cytoplasm layer and the nucleus at the edge.
Chloroplast: draw one or more small oval organelles (smaller than the nucleus, about a quarter of its diameter) in the cytoplasm near the cell wall, with internal grana, and label chloroplast.

Amyloplast: draw a small round or oval organelle of a similar size, with dots (starch granules) inside, in the cytoplasm and label amyloplast; all three should be inside the cell wall and have label lines.

questions.question: State the function of the organelle shown in the electron micrograph of a plant cell.
questions.answer: The organelle is the Golgi apparatus; it modifies and packages proteins (and lipids) into vesicles for secretion or use in the cell.
steps: The electron micrograph shows a stack of flattened, curved membrane-bound sacs with vesicles at the edges, which is the Golgi apparatus.

Its function is to modify proteins (for example by adding carbohydrate to make glycoproteins), and package them in vesicles that are carried to the cell surface membrane for secretion; in plants it also makes cell wall materials.

questions.question: Complete the table showing in which domains (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya) given structures would be found.
questions.answer: Cell membrane: more than one domain; nucleolus: Eukarya only; cell wall: more than one domain; 70S ribosome: more than one domain.
steps: A cell surface membrane is found in all cells, so it is in more than one domain.
The nucleolus is found in the nucleus, so only in Eukarya.
Cell walls are found in Bacteria (peptidoglycan), Archaea and in plants and fungi (Eukarya), so more than one domain.
70S ribosomes are found in Archaea and Bacteria (and in mitochondria and chloroplasts), whereas the cytoplasm of Eukarya has 80S ribosomes, so more than one domain.

questions.question: How many of the three domains contain prokaryotic organisms? A none B one C two D three.
questions.answer: C two
steps: Archaea and Bacteria contain prokaryotic organisms.
Eukarya contains organisms with eukaryotic cells.
Two domains are prokaryotic.
So the answer is C, two.

questions.question: Complete the diagram of a prokaryotic cell by drawing and labelling a flagellum and a plasmid.
questions.answer: Draw and label a long curved flagellum attached to the cell surface, and a small circle (plasmid) in the cytoplasm.
steps: Flagellum: draw a long, wavy or spiral thread that starts at the cell surface, passes through the cell wall and extends well out of the cell (longer than the pili), and label it flagellum.
Plasmid: draw a small separate ring (circle) inside the cell, in the cytoplasm and away from the main chromosome, and label it plasmid.

questions.question: State the function of a plasmid.
questions.answer: Carries extra genes (such as antibiotic resistance) as small circular DNA, which can pass between bacteria.
steps: A plasmid is a small circular piece of DNA separate from the main chromosome.
It carries non-essential genes such as antibiotic resistance.
Plasmids can be transferred between bacteria.
This gives the bacterium extra characteristics that may help it survive.

questions.question: Give one difference between prokaryotic ribosomes and eukaryotic ribosomes.
questions.answer: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S; eukaryotic ribosomes are larger 80S.
steps: Prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller, measured as 70S.
Eukaryotic ribosomes are larger, measured as 80S.
Both carry out protein synthesis.
The size difference is the key difference.

questions.question: How many of these statements about eukaryotic ribosomes are correct? On the surface of both types of ER; inside chloroplasts and mitochondria; involved in transcription. A none B one C two D three.
questions.answer: A none
steps: Smooth ER has no ribosomes on its surface, so statement one is wrong.
Eukaryotic ribosomes (80S) are in the cytoplasm, not in chloroplasts or mitochondria, so statement two is wrong.
Transcription happens in the nucleus; ribosomes carry out translation, so statement three is wrong.
No statements are correct, so the answer is A.

questions.question: Which term describes the Hawaii palila honeycreeper being found only in mountainous forest on one island? A diversity B endemic C polygenic D specific.
questions.answer: B endemic
steps: Endemic means found only in one restricted area.
The palila is found only on one island.
Diversity means variety, not location.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: The palila population was 7100 in 2003 and 950 in 2020. Calculate the percentage change, to two significant figures.
questions.answer: -87 % (a decrease)
steps: Percentage change = -6150 / 7100 x 100 = -86.6 %.
To two significant figures this is -87 %.
The population has decreased by about 87 %.

questions.question: Explain how the Hawaii amakihi and palila honeycreepers could have evolved from the same common ancestor, using the table.
questions.answer: An ancestral honeycreeper population reached the islands and split into populations in different habitats with different foods; natural selection acted differently on each, so they diverged until they could no longer interbreed, forming separate species.
steps: The two species share a common ancestor: a population of ancestral honeycreepers colonised the Hawaiian islands and spread, so some populations became separated on different islands and in different habitats (geographical isolation and ecological isolation).

The table shows differences in selection pressure: amakihi live in lowland and mountainous forest and shrubland on 3 islands and eat nectar, tree sap, spiders and insects, whereas palila live only in mountainous forest on 1 island and eat seeds and berries.

Random mutations produced different alleles (for example for bill shape and size); individuals whose alleles suited the local food (for example a strong bill for seeds) survived and reproduced more, so those alleles increased in frequency (natural selection) and each population became adapted to its own habitat and food.
Different habitats and the small size of the palila population (fewer than 1000 birds) also mean allele frequencies changed by genetic drift and the founder effect.

After many generations the gene pools were so different that the birds could no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring (reproductive isolation), so they are now different species (allopatric speciation, with possibly some sympatric divergence in food).

questions.question: Explain how scientists could determine which of the 17 other honeycreeper species is most closely related to the palila.
questions.answer: Compare DNA base sequences of each species with the palila; the species with the most similar sequences is most closely related.
steps: Extract DNA from each honeycreeper species.
Sequence the same gene or region in each species and in the palila.
Compare base sequences and count differences.
The species with the fewest differences is the most closely related.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term species richness.
questions.answer: The number of different species in an area or habitat.
steps: Species richness counts how many different species are present.
It does not depend on how many individuals there are.
It is a measure of biodiversity in a habitat.
Higher species richness means a more varied habitat.

questions.question: Describe how new cichlid species may have formed in the four lakes and how scientists would have determined that the cichlids were six different species.
questions.answer: Populations were isolated in different lakes, so selection and mutation led to divergence and reproductive isolation; species were identified by morphology, breeding tests and DNA.
steps: Cichlids colonised new crater lakes, where some populations became geographically isolated.
Different conditions and food sources cause different selection pressures.
Mutations and natural selection cause the populations to diverge genetically.
Reproductive isolation prevents gene flow, so the populations become separate species.
Scientists identify species using morphological differences and breeding tests.
Molecular (DNA) evidence confirms that the populations are genetically distinct species.

questions.question: Using the table and formula, determine which crater lake has the higher cichlid biodiversity, given D = 2.8 for Lake Xiloa.
questions.answer: Lake Apoyo has the higher cichlid biodiversity: D = 3.1 compared with 2.8 for Lake Xiloa (D = 3.05).
steps: Fill in the missing value for A. zaliosus: n(n - 1) = 12 x 11 = 132.
D = 99 540 / 32 626 = 3.05, so D is about 3.1 for Lake Apoyo.
A higher index of diversity means higher biodiversity, so Lake Apoyo (3.1) is more diverse than Lake Xiloa (2.8).

questions.question: In a later study, 672 cichlids were gold (dominant phenotype) and 128 were melanic (recessive). With the first study p = 0.6 and q = 0.4, determine whether the allele frequencies have changed.
questions.answer: No change: q^2 = 128 / 800 = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 0.6, the same as the first study.
steps: Total fish = 672 + 128 = 800.
Melanic (recessive) fish are q^2, so q^2 = 128 / 800 = 0.16.
q = square root of 0.16 = 0.4, and p = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6.
These match the first study, so the allele frequencies have not changed.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term species richness, as used for Sumatra.
questions.answer: The number of different species in an area.
steps: Species richness is a count of the different species present.
A region with high species richness has many species.
It does not measure how many individuals each species has.
Sumatra has many species, so its species richness is high.

questions.question: Explain the advantages of drying seeds before they are frozen for storage.
questions.answer: Low water content reduces metabolism and decay, and prevents ice crystals forming that would damage the seeds on freezing.
steps: Drying reduces the water content of the seeds.
Less water means slower metabolism and less enzyme activity, so seeds stay viable longer.
Without water, ice crystals cannot form, so cell membranes and structures are not damaged on freezing.
Dry seeds are less likely to be attacked by fungi or microbes.

questions.question: Write the equation for the heterozygosity index.
questions.answer: H = number of heterozygotes / total number of individuals in the sample.
steps: Heterozygotes are individuals with two different alleles for a gene.
Count the number of heterozygous individuals in the sample.
Divide by the total number of individuals sampled.
The result is a value between 0 and 1 that shows genetic diversity.

questions.question: The heterozygosity index of 500 titan arum plants in botanical gardens is 0.166. Calculate the number of heterozygotes.
steps: H = heterozygotes / total, so heterozygotes = H x total.
Heterozygotes = 0.166 x 500 = 83.
Round to a whole number of plants.
So there are 83 heterozygotes.

questions.question: Discuss the suggestions for conserving the titan arum without losing genetic diversity: growing asexually produced plants, storing pollen, creating a studbook and artificial pollination.
questions.answer: Each suggestion has benefits and drawbacks: clones are quick but lower diversity, pollen storage and studbooks preserve diversity, and artificial pollination ensures seed set.
steps: Asexual propagation is quick and cheap, but produces clones with low genetic diversity.
Storing pollen when flowers open preserves genetic material from a rare flowering event.
A studbook records parentage so breeding can avoid inbreeding and keep alleles.
Artificial pollination helps seed production because the flowers last only two to three days and insects may be absent.
Using both wild and botanical garden plants combines genetic sources.
Together these methods are more effective than any single approach, but each needs cost and expertise.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term niche.
questions.answer: The role of an organism in its environment, including its habitat, food and interactions with other organisms.
steps: A niche describes how an organism lives and its role in the ecosystem.
It includes habitat, food source, and predators or competitors.
No two species occupy exactly the same niche in a stable community.
So the niche is the organism's total role in its environment.

questions.question: The mimic octopus has the same banding pattern as the venomous sea snake. Name this type of adaptation.
questions.answer: Mimicry.
steps: The octopus copies the appearance of a different, dangerous animal.
This copying of appearance is called mimicry.
Predators avoid the octopus because it resembles a venomous snake.
So the adaptation is mimicry.

questions.question: Suggest why the mimic octopus would change its appearance to look like a flat fish and like a venomous sea snake.
questions.answer: Looking like a flat fish helps it blend in and hide from predators; looking like a venomous snake makes predators avoid it.
steps: Looking like a flat fish helps the octopus camouflage itself on the seabed.
This makes it harder for predators to spot.
Looking like a venomous sea snake deters predators that avoid dangerous prey.
Changing appearance lets the octopus avoid predators in different situations.

questions.question: Which describes the purpose of the current pain-relieving drug in stage II of the drug trial? A control B digitalis C placebo D solvent.
questions.answer: A control
steps: The current drug is an existing treatment used for comparison with tetrodotoxin.
This comparison group is the control.
A placebo has no active drug, so it is not the current treatment.
So the answer is A, control.

questions.question: Describe the processes that would occur before and after stage II of the tetrodotoxin drug trial.
questions.answer: Before stage II: laboratory and animal testing, plus stage I safety trials; after: larger stage III trials, then regulatory approval and monitoring.
steps: Before stage II, the drug is tested in cells and animals for safety and toxicity.
Stage I tests safety and dosage in a small group of healthy volunteers.
After stage II, a larger stage III trial compares the drug in more patients.
Results are peer reviewed, and approval is given only if the drug is safe and effective.

questions.question: Using the graph of pain relief duration for tetrodotoxin and the current drug, comment on the results.
questions.answer: Tetrodotoxin gives pain relief for much longer than the current drug: it works for up to about 450 hours (a few patients), while the current drug stops working by about 20 to 30 hours; most patients get less than 50 hours of relief with either drug.
steps: Both curves fall steeply: most patients have a short period of pain relief (for most, the number of patients with long relief is very low).
The current drug (dashed line) falls to zero by about 25 to 30 hours, so nobody has relief for longer than about a day.

Tetrodotoxin (solid line) has a long tail: a small number of patients still have pain relief at 100 hours, 200 hours and up to about 450 hours, which is more than 15 times as long as for the current drug.

So tetrodotoxin appears to be more effective at providing long-lasting relief; but the graph does not give the number of patients, the dose, side effects or the average, and there is no statistical test, so a large phase III trial is needed.

questions.question: Calculate the expected mass of eggplants imported by France in 2023, given the 2020 mass in the table and a 1.6 % annual increase.
questions.answer: 55 472 tonnes
steps: France imported 52 892 tonnes in 2020, and the increase of 1.6% per year is compounded, so multiply by 1.016 each year.
To the nearest whole number the mass is 55 472 tonnes.

questions.question: How many of the eggplant varieties tested were categorised as susceptible to R. solanacearum? A none B one C two D three.
questions.answer: C: two
steps: Susceptible means a disease index (DI) of more than 50.
Variety B has DI 61.3 and variety C has DI 89.2, so these are susceptible; A (45.8) is moderately susceptible and D (9.2) is resistant.
So two varieties are susceptible.

questions.question: Explain how seed banks would prepare, store and assess the viability of seeds of closely related wild plants.
questions.answer: Clean and dry the seeds, store them cold in sealed containers, and test viability by germinating samples at intervals.
steps: Seeds are collected, cleaned and dried to reduce water content.
Dry seeds are stored at low temperature, often frozen, to slow metabolism.
Seeds are kept in sealed containers to prevent moisture and pests.
Samples are germinated regularly to measure the percentage that grow, which shows viability.

questions.question: Explain how scientists could breed new high-yielding eggplant varieties that are resistant to R. solanacearum, using the tables.
questions.answer: Cross a resistant variety with a high-yielding variety, select offspring with both traits, and backcross to keep high yield.
steps: Identify a resistant variety with a low disease index from the seed bank.
Cross it with a high-yielding variety to combine the two sets of alleles.
Test offspring for disease resistance (disease index) and yield.
Select the best plants and repeat crosses (backcrossing) to fix both traits.

questions.question: Name the domain that would contain the algae with chloroplasts shown in photograph A.
questions.answer: Eukarya.
steps: Algae are eukaryotic organisms.
Chloroplasts are membrane-bound organelles found in eukaryotic cells.
Prokaryotes do not have membrane-bound organelles like chloroplasts.
So the domain is Eukarya.

questions.question: Calculate the magnification of the chloroplast shown in photograph B, to two significant figures.
steps: Magnification = length of scale bar in the image / actual length it represents.
The 1.5 um bar measures about 25 mm on the printed page (88 px at 745 px per 210 mm = 24.8 mm); a ruler should give 24 mm to 26 mm.
Convert: 25 mm = 25 000 um, so magnification = 25 000 / 1.5 = 16 667, which is x17 000 to 2 significant figures (16 537 using 24.8 mm).

questions.question: Explain why the microscope used for photograph B shows more detail than the microscope used for photograph A.
questions.answer: An electron microscope has a shorter wavelength than light, giving higher resolution and more detail.
steps: Resolution is the ability to distinguish two points as separate.
Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light.
A shorter wavelength gives higher resolution.
So the electron microscope in B shows finer detail than the light microscope in A.

questions.question: Which is another structure that contains starch? A amyloplast B plasmodesmata C tonoplast D vacuole.
questions.answer: A amyloplast
steps: Amyloplasts are plastids that store starch.
Plasmodesmata are channels between cells and do not store starch.
The tonoplast is the membrane around the vacuole, not a store of starch.
So the answer is A, amyloplast.

questions.question: Name and give the function of the animal-cell structure shown in the photograph of algal cells.
questions.answer: Centriole (a ring of nine triplets of microtubules); it makes the spindle fibres (organises microtubules) for nuclear division.
steps: The photograph shows a small cylinder seen end-on, made of a ring of nine triplets of microtubules with no membrane, which is a centriole.

Centrioles organise the microtubules that form the spindle during mitosis and meiosis, so that chromosomes or chromatids are pulled apart (in some algae and animal cells they also form the base of cilia and flagella).

questions.question: Which term describes the fish being found only in Lake Tanganyika? A diversity B endemic C homozygous D specific.
questions.answer: B endemic
steps: Endemic means found only in one restricted area.
The humphead cichlid is found only in Lake Tanganyika.
Homozygous describes genotype, not location.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: Suggest why female humphead cichlids keep fertilised eggs in their mouths, and give a reason.
questions.answer: It protects the eggs from predators and infection, so more offspring survive to hatch.
steps: Keeping eggs in the mouth hides them from predators.
The mother can guard them while they develop.
Protected eggs are less likely to be eaten or damaged.
More offspring survive to hatch, increasing reproductive success.

questions.question: State the relationship shown in the graph between mean sperm length and swimming speed of 30 cichlid species.
questions.answer: Positive correlation: the longer the sperm cell, the faster it swims.
steps: The points rise from about 50 um s^-1 at about 14.5 um length to about 70 to 90 um s^-1 at lengths of 24 to 32 um.

So as the mean sperm length increases the mean swimming speed increases (a positive correlation), although the points are scattered and the relationship is stronger at short lengths than at long ones.

questions.question: Which statistical test should be used to assess the strength of the relationship between sperm length and swimming speed? A chi-squared test B correlation coefficient C index of diversity D Student's t-test.
questions.answer: B correlation coefficient
steps: A correlation coefficient measures the strength of a relationship between two continuous variables.
A chi-squared test checks association between categorical data.
The index of diversity is not a statistical test.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: Suggest one advantage for a male cichlid of producing sperm cells with faster swimming speed.
questions.answer: Faster sperm reach the egg sooner, increasing the chance of fertilisation.
steps: Sperm must swim to reach the egg.
Faster sperm arrive earlier, before competing sperm.
Arriving first increases the chance of fertilising the egg.
So the male has greater reproductive success.

questions.question: Which labelled structure (W, X, Y or Z) in the diagram of a sperm cell is the acrosome?
questions.answer: A: W
