steps: The acrosome is a membrane-bound sac (a specialised lysosome) that caps the front of the sperm head, over the nucleus, and contains hydrolytic enzymes.
W points to the clear sac-like cap at the front of the head, which is the acrosome.
X points to the cell surface membrane and cytoplasm at the outside of the head, Y is the nucleus and Z is the mid-piece containing mitochondria.

questions.question: Calculate the magnification of the sperm cell shown in the diagram, to two significant figures.
steps: Magnification = length of scale bar in the image / actual length it represents.
The 60 um scale bar measures about 45 mm on the printed page (159 px at 745 px per 210 mm = 44.8 mm); a ruler should give 44 mm to 46 mm.
Convert: 45 mm = 45 000 um, so magnification = 45 000 / 60 = 750 (x750 to 2 s.f.).

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure and function of lysosomes and acrosomes.
questions.answer: Both are membrane-bound vesicles of hydrolytic enzymes; lysosomes digest material inside the cell, while the acrosome releases enzymes to digest the egg coat.
steps: Both are membrane-bound vesicles containing hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes.
Lysosomes are found throughout the cell and digest waste or pathogens inside it.
The acrosome sits at the tip of the sperm head and is a specialised lysosome.
The acrosome releases enzymes outside the cell to digest the zona pellucida so the sperm can enter the egg.

questions.question: Give the names of the other two domains, apart from Bacteria.
questions.answer: Archaea and Eukarya.
steps: The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
Bacteria is given, so the other two are the remaining domains.
Archaea is one of these.
Eukarya is the other.

questions.question: A T. magnifica cell is 20 mm long and M. genitalium is 300 nm long. Calculate how many times larger T. magnifica is, in standard form.
questions.answer: 6.7 x 10^4 times.
steps: Convert 20 mm to nm: 20 mm = 20 x 10^6 nm = 2 x 10^7 nm.
In standard form this is 6.7 x 10^4.
So T. magnifica is about 6.7 x 10^4 times larger.

questions.question: Explain how the circular DNA, ribosomes and membrane of a pepin each contribute to its function of protein synthesis.
questions.answer: Circular DNA carries the genes for proteins; ribosomes translate mRNA into polypeptides; the membrane encloses the structure and controls what enters and leaves.
steps: Circular DNA carries the genetic code for the proteins to be made.
Its genes are transcribed to mRNA.
Ribosomes read the mRNA and join amino acids to form polypeptides by translation.
The membrane encloses the pepin and controls the entry of amino acids and the exit of products.

questions.question: Explain why an optimum temperature and water are needed for bacterial growth.
questions.answer: Enzymes controlling metabolism work best at the optimum temperature, and water is needed as a solvent and reactant for metabolic reactions.
steps: Enzymes controlling growth and metabolism work fastest at an optimum temperature.
Temperatures above or below this slow the rate of metabolic reactions.
Water is the solvent for cytoplasmic reactions and is needed for cell growth.
Without water, metabolic reactions and cell growth cannot take place.

questions.question: Explain the results for bacteria A and B shown in the graph of growth rate against oxygen concentration.
questions.answer: Bacteria A grows best at low oxygen (about 1%), and growth falls to zero by about 3.3% because higher oxygen is harmful (microaerophile); bacteria B grows faster as oxygen rises up to about 1.5% and then stays at the maximum, so it needs oxygen (obligate aerobe).
steps: Bacteria B: growth rate is almost zero with no oxygen, rises steeply as oxygen increases to about 1.5%, and then levels off (a plateau) up to 5%; it needs oxygen for aerobic respiration to make ATP, and growth is then limited by other factors.

Bacteria A: growth rate is highest at 0 to 1.5% oxygen (growth occurs with little oxygen), and falls sharply above about 1.5% to 2% to zero at about 3.3%; so it needs only a little oxygen and is damaged by higher concentrations (a microaerophile, or oxygen produces toxic free radicals).
So the two types differ in their tolerance of oxygen: B is an aerobe, A is intolerant of high concentrations of oxygen; the scatter in A's points at about 1.5% shows variation between repeats.

questions.question: Give one reason for a named anatomical adaptation of the snow leopard that enables it to occupy its niche.
questions.answer: Thick fur, which insulates the snow leopard against the cold mountain environment.
steps: The snow leopard lives in cold, snowy mountains.
Its thick fur traps air and insulates the body.
This reduces heat loss and keeps the animal warm.
So thick fur helps it survive in its niche.

questions.question: Describe how the biodiversity of the habitats in the areas where snow leopards live could be compared.
questions.answer: Use the same sampling method in each area and compare species richness and an index of diversity.
steps: Choose the same sampling method, such as quadrats or transects, in each area.
Count the number of different species in each area to find species richness.
Calculate the index of diversity for each area using the number of individuals of each species.
Compare the values; the area with the higher value has greater biodiversity.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of wild snow leopards from 2002 to 2022, using the graph, to one decimal place.
steps: Read the graph: about 7100 snow leopards in 2002 and about 1200 in 2022.
Percentage decrease = 5900 / 7100 x 100 = 83.1%.

questions.question: Suggest one reason for the decrease in the number of snow leopards.
questions.answer: Poaching for fur and body parts, or loss of habitat and prey.
steps: Snow leopards are hunted illegally for their fur and body parts.
Habitat is lost to farming, roads and development.
Loss of prey such as wild sheep and goats reduces food supply.
Any one of these reduces the population.

questions.question: Using the map scale, calculate the width of the desert region shown by line X, in km, in standard form.
questions.answer: About 3 x 10^2 km (about 320 km)
steps: The scale bar shows that 1000 km is about 86 px on this page (0 to 1000), and line X is about 27 to 28 px long.
Width = 27.5 / 86 x 1000 = about 320 km (for a ruler measurement, compare X with the 1000 km bar).
In standard form this is about 3.2 x 10^2 km (3 x 10^2 km to 1 significant figure).

questions.question: Explain how the snow leopard subspecies could have formed, using the information in the question.
questions.answer: Geographic isolation by deserts and mountains stops gene flow, so mutation and different selection pressures cause the populations to diverge.
steps: Populations became separated by geographic barriers such as deserts and mountains.
Gene flow between the separated populations stopped.
Each population experienced different environmental conditions.
Mutations arose independently in each population.
Natural selection favoured different alleles in each environment.
Over time the populations accumulated different characteristics and became subspecies.

questions.question: Give a reason why these populations are described as subspecies rather than different species.
questions.answer: They can still interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
steps: A subspecies is a population that differs in characteristics from others.
Different species cannot produce fertile offspring together.
The snow leopard subspecies can interbreed and produce fertile young.
So they remain subspecies of one species.

questions.question: Which row of the table describes the markings, poisons and body inflation of Canthigaster valenti?
questions.answer: B: anatomical, physiological, behavioural
steps: The markings on the skin (the colour and pattern) are a structural feature, so they are anatomical.
Production of poison is a biochemical process in the body, so it is physiological.
Inflating the body is the way the fish acts when threatened, so it is behavioural: row B.

questions.question: Explain how the appearance of the non-poisonous fish Paraluteres prionurus shows it is adapted to its habitat.
questions.answer: It resembles the poisonous Canthigaster, so predators avoid it, which protects the non-poisonous fish.
steps: Paraluteres is not poisonous, so it cannot defend itself with toxins.
Its appearance closely resembles the poisonous Canthigaster valenti.
Predators learn to avoid the warning appearance of the poisonous fish.
They therefore also avoid Paraluteres, which is a form of mimicry that protects it.

questions.question: Explain why Canthigaster valenti and Paraluteres prionurus are unable to reproduce with each other.
questions.answer: They are different species, so their gametes are incompatible or their mating behaviour and genetics prevent fertile offspring.
steps: The two fish are different species.
Different species have different genetic makeup and gametes that may not fuse.
Mating behaviour and timing may also differ, preventing mating.
Any hybrid offspring would be infertile, so they cannot reproduce with each other.

questions.question: A recessive mutant allele of the ARD1 gene causes arginase deficiency. It was suggested that this mutant allele arose in meiosis during prophase I. Suggest how this mutant allele could be produced in prophase I.
questions.answer: By unequal crossing over: at a chiasma the non-sister chromatids break and rejoin at slightly different points within the ARD1 gene, so bases are deleted or duplicated and the base sequence of the allele is changed.
steps: In prophase I homologous chromosomes pair up and non-sister chromatids form chiasmata (crossing over).
At a chiasma the chromatids break and rejoin to exchange sections of DNA.
If the breaks are not at exactly matching points (unequal crossing over) and fall within the ARD1 gene, bases are lost from one chromatid and gained by the other.
This deletion or insertion of bases changes the base sequence of the gene (for example a frameshift), producing the mutant ARD1 allele.

questions.question: The incidence of arginase deficiency is 1 in 300 000 in a population of 7 800 000 000, so 26 000 people have it. Calculate how many people do not have a mutant allele.
questions.answer: About 7.77 x 10^9 people (approx 7 771 500 000).
steps: p^2 = 0.996, the frequency of people with no mutant allele.

questions.question: Give two differences between active mRNA and pre-mRNA.
questions.answer: Pre-mRNA contains introns that are removed in mature mRNA, and mature mRNA has a 5' cap and poly-A tail added.
steps: Pre-mRNA is the primary transcript and contains introns.
Introns are non-coding and are removed by splicing to make mature mRNA.
Mature mRNA has a 5' cap added to its start.
Mature mRNA has a poly-A tail added to its end.

questions.question: Explain how a pluripotent stem cell could become a cell that synthesises arginase.
questions.answer: Signals switch on the arginase gene in differentiating liver-type cells, which is transcribed and translated into arginase.
steps: Chemical signals from the environment cause the stem cell to differentiate.
Genes are switched on or off, so only the arginase gene is expressed in the liver-type cell.
The arginase gene is transcribed to pre-mRNA, which is processed to mRNA.
mRNA leaves the nucleus and is translated by ribosomes into arginase.
The enzyme is folded and processed in the ER and Golgi before secretion.

questions.question: Explain why society may support the use of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) to treat patients with arginase deficiency.
questions.answer: hiPSCs are made from adult skin cells, so no embryos are destroyed, and they can potentially cure the disease with fewer ethical objections.
steps: hiPSCs are made by reprogramming adult skin cells.
No embryos need to be destroyed, which avoids major ethical objections.
They can be grown in large numbers and used to treat genetic disease.
Patients could receive cells that match their own genes, reducing rejection risk.

questions.question: Which statement describes biodiversity? A species richness of only the endemic species within a habitat B species richness of all the species within a habitat C the role of only the endemic species D the role of all the species.
questions.answer: B species richness of all the species within a habitat
steps: Biodiversity includes all species, not only endemic ones.
It is measured by species richness, which counts all species in a habitat.
Options A and C restrict the count to endemic species, which is too narrow.
Option D describes roles, not biodiversity, so the answer is B.

questions.question: Describe the changes in biodiversity along the Rideau River, using the graph of biodiversity index values.
questions.answer: Overall biodiversity falls downstream: Section 4 is poorest (birds moderate, mussels poor at 0.4, plants moderate at 0.5), while fish stay highest in every section (2.5 to 2.9) and mussels fall steadily from 1.4 to 0.4.
steps: Birds: the index is 1.6 in Section 1 and 1.5 in Sections 2 and 3 (good biodiversity), but falls to 1.0 in Section 4, which is only moderate biodiversity.

Fish: the index is the highest of any group in every section (2.5, 2.9, 2.6 and 2.5), with a peak in Section 2 where it is good; in the other sections it is moderate (a high value does not mean good biodiversity because the categories differ between groups).
Mussels: biodiversity decreases along the river, from 1.4 (good) in Section 1 to 0.7 (moderate) in Sections 2 and 3 and 0.4 (poor) in Section 4, which is the only poor category.
Aquatic plants: 0.9 in Section 1 and 1.0 in Section 2 (good), no data in Section 3, and 0.5 (moderate) in Section 4, so the biodiversity of plants is also lower at the end.

So Section 1 has the best overall biodiversity (3 good and 1 moderate) and Section 4 the worst (no good, 3 moderate and 1 poor); the cause could be pollution or human activity increasing downstream, but the graph alone does not show this.

questions.question: Birds have an index of 1.6 (good) and fish 2.5 (moderate) in Section 1. Suggest why the fish have moderate biodiversity but a greater index value.
questions.answer: Each group has its own categories and ranges, so index values can only be compared within one group, not between groups.
steps: Biodiversity index values are used to compare within one group of organisms.
Categories (good, moderate, poor) are set using different ranges for each group.
So the fish's higher index value does not mean it has better biodiversity than birds.
Fish's moderate category is judged against fish-specific thresholds.

questions.question: Complete the student's table of data for aquatic plants in Section 3.
steps: For each species (n = 8, 6, 3, 2, 9, 2, 2, 6, 5, 2, 3 in the order of the table), subtract 1 to get (n - 1): 7, 5, 2, 1, 8, 1, 1, 5, 4, 1, 2.

questions.question: Calculate the biodiversity index value for aquatic plants in Section 3 of the river using the student's table.
State what is meant by the term endemic, as applied to Baird's tapir.
questions.answer: Found naturally in only one restricted area or country and nowhere else.
steps: Endemic means a species is restricted to one geographic area.
Baird's tapir is found naturally only in certain countries of Central America.
It does not occur naturally anywhere else.
So endemic means restricted to this region.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage decrease in Baird's tapir numbers from 5500 in 2006 to 3000 in 2016.
questions.answer: 45.5 % decrease.
steps: Percentage change = -2500 / 5500 x 100 = -45.45 %.
This is a decrease, so write 45.5 % to one decimal place.
The population fell by 45.5 % over the 10 years.

questions.question: Explain how human activity other than hunting could have caused the decrease in Baird's tapir numbers.
questions.answer: Habitat loss from deforestation and agriculture, fragmentation of forests, and pollution reduce food and breeding sites.
steps: Forests are cleared for farming and development, so the tapir's habitat is lost.
Fragmented forest isolates tapir populations, reducing breeding opportunities.
Roads cause road deaths and further divide habitat.
Loss of habitat reduces food and shelter, so fewer tapirs survive.

questions.question: Describe how each of the effects of freezing on the tapir sperm, listed in the table, could be determined.
questions.answer: Moving: observe a sample under a light microscope and count the percentage that move; straight-line swimming: record the paths of sperm (video or time-lapse) and measure how straight they are; acrosome: stain the sperm and count the percentage with an intact acrosome under a microscope.
steps: Percentage of sperm capable of moving: put a drop of sperm on a slide and observe under a light microscope, counting moving and non-moving sperm in a number of fields of view, then calculate the percentage that move.

Ability to swim in a straight line: video or time-lapse photograph the swimming sperm and trace their paths, then measure how straight the paths are (for example the straight-line distance compared with the path length), and take the mean for many sperm.

Percentage with an undamaged acrosome: stain the sperm so that the acrosome can be seen (or use a stain or antibody specific to it), view with a microscope and count the number with a complete acrosome out of the total.
Compare freshly collected and frozen then thawed samples, using the same number of sperm and repeats.

questions.question: Explain how freezing sperm could affect the success of captive breeding programmes.
questions.answer: Freezing can damage sperm and reduce motility, but frozen sperm can be stored long term, preserving genetic diversity and allowing breeding with distant males.
steps: Ice crystals can damage sperm membranes, reducing motility and viability.
Lower sperm quality reduces fertilisation and pregnancy success.
Frozen sperm can be stored for years, so samples from dead or distant males remain available.
Using stored sperm allows breeding between unrelated individuals, which maintains genetic diversity.

questions.question: State the letter that shows the zona pellucida on the student's diagram of a human egg cell.
questions.answer: Z
steps: The zona pellucida is the layer of glycoproteins that surrounds the egg cell membrane and lies inside the layer of follicle cells.
W points to one of the outer follicle cells (corona radiata), X points to the egg cytoplasm and Y points to the nucleus.
Z points to the pale outer layer between the follicle cells and the cell, which is the zona pellucida.

questions.question: Name the structures that contain enzymes involved in hardening the zona pellucida.
questions.answer: Cortical granules.
steps: Cortical granules lie just under the egg cell membrane.
They are released after fertilisation.
They contain enzymes that harden the zona pellucida.
So the structures are cortical granules.

questions.question: How many of these statements about sperm cells are correct? Mid-piece has many mitochondria for anaerobic respiration; acrosome is a membrane-bound sac with digestive enzymes; nucleus contains circular DNA. A none B one C two D three.
questions.answer: B one
steps: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, so statement one is wrong.
The acrosome is a membrane-bound sac with digestive enzymes, so statement two is correct.
The sperm nucleus contains linear DNA in chromosomes, so statement three is wrong.
Only one statement is correct, so the answer is B.

questions.question: Calculate the acrosome to nucleus ratio for the reed bunting sperm cell shown in the table.
steps: Measure the acrosome and the nucleus on the reed bunting drawing (the two lines on the right): the acrosome is about 115 mm and the nucleus about 26 mm on the printed page (409 px and 94 px).
Ratio = acrosome length / nucleus length = 409 / 94 = 4.35.
So the acrosome to nucleus ratio is about 4.4 : 1 (a ruler measurement should give about 4.3 to 4.4).

questions.question: Explain how the acrosome to nucleus ratio and helical membrane width are related to the reproductive behaviour of these birds, using the table and graph.
questions.answer: The reed bunting female mates with several males, so sperm compete; its sperm have a larger acrosome to nucleus ratio (about 4.4 against 0.7) and a wider helical membrane, which make them swim faster and more likely to fertilise the egg first, whereas the nuthatch has one partner so there is no sperm competition.
steps: The nuthatch female has one male partner, so there is no sperm competition; the nuthatch sperm has a narrow helical membrane and a small acrosome to nucleus ratio (about 0.7).

The reed bunting female mates with several males in a short time, so the sperm of different males compete to fertilise the egg; its sperm have a wide helical membrane and a large acrosome to nucleus ratio (about 4.4).

The graph shows that as the width of the helical membrane increases the swimming speed increases from about 70 to about 115 um s^-1 (about 64% faster), levelling off at the widest membranes; the ratio of acrosome to nucleus also increases speed.

Faster sperm are more likely to reach and fertilise the egg first, so males with these sperm have greater reproductive success and pass on the alleles for them (sexual selection), so sperm competition has selected for these adaptations in the reed bunting.

questions.question: Suggest reasons why it may be advantageous for blue dragon sea slugs to be hermaphrodites.
questions.answer: Every individual can produce offspring, so mating is possible even when partners are scarce, and both partners can gain offspring.
steps: Blue dragons are sparse in the ocean, so finding a mate can be difficult.
Being hermaphrodite means any encounter can produce offspring for both animals.
Each individual can produce both eggs and sperm, which maximises reproductive output.
Mating with another individual gives genetic mixing, which increases genetic diversity.

questions.question: Complete the table showing how many of 100 cats would be homozygous dominant and how many heterozygous, using p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1.
questions.answer: BB: 36 cats; Bb: 48 cats
steps: bb = q^2 = 16 / 100 = 0.16, so q = square root of 0.16 = 0.4.
Number of cats: BB = 0.36 x 100 = 36 and Bb = 0.48 x 100 = 48 (check: 36 + 48 + 16 = 100).

questions.question: Bacteria is one domain with prokaryotic cells. Name the other domain that has prokaryotic cells.
questions.answer: Archaea.
steps: Prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Bacteria is one domain of prokaryotes.
Archaea is the only other prokaryotic domain.
So the answer is Archaea.

questions.question: Draw three labelled features on the outline diagram of a bacterial cell that may be found in a prokaryotic cell.
questions.answer: Any three of: flagellum, plasmid (small ring of DNA), capsule, pili, ribosomes (70S), circular DNA (nucleoid), each drawn inside or on the cell and labelled.
steps: Plasmid: draw a small separate ring (circle) in the cytoplasm and label it plasmid.
Circular DNA (nucleoid): draw a larger coiled loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm, with no membrane around it, and label it circular DNA or nucleoid.

Flagellum: draw a long wavy thread attached to the surface passing out through the cell wall, labelled flagellum; or capsule: a slime layer outside the cell wall; or pili: short thin hairs on the surface; or small dots labelled ribosomes (70S) in the cytoplasm.

questions.question: Explain the distribution of bacteria in the human digestive system, using the organ diagram and table of conditions.
questions.answer: Numbers rise from the stomach (10^3 per cm^3) to the colon (10^12 per cm^3) because pH becomes less acidic, oxygen falls and food stays for longer; each type of bacterium is found where the pH and oxygen suit it.
steps: Stomach: the pH is 1 to 3 (very acidic), which denatures the enzymes of most bacteria and kills them, and the oxygen content is high, so only 10^3 bacteria per cm^3 and acid-tolerant types such as Lactobacillus and Helicobacter survive.

Duodenum: the pH is 6 to 7 (close to neutral), but food moves through quickly and enzymes and bile are secreted, so the number is still low (10^3); Lactobacillus and Streptococcus can tolerate the oxygen present.

Ileum: pH 6 to 8 is close to the optimum for many enzymes, and oxygen is lower, so numbers are much higher (10^7), with a wider range of types, including anaerobes such as Clostridium and Bacteroides that cannot grow with a lot of oxygen.

Colon: oxygen is lowest, so strict anaerobes (Clostridium, Bacteroides) grow best, the pH of 5 to 7 is suitable, and food stays a long time (with undigested material to feed on), so the number is the highest (10^12 per cm^3).
So the pH and oxygen content (together with nutrients and food transit time) determine which species can grow and how many there are in each organ.

questions.question: Explain two anatomical adaptations of gentoo penguins that help them survive in very cold Antarctic waters.
questions.answer: A thick layer of blubber and dense waterproof feathers insulate the penguin; a streamlined body and flippers help it swim in search of food.
steps: Adaptation 1: a thick layer of blubber under the skin.
Reason: blubber insulates the body and reduces heat loss in cold water.
Adaptation 2: a streamlined body with flipper-shaped wings.
Reason: this reduces drag so the penguin can swim efficiently to catch fish, squid and shrimp.

questions.question: Suggest one way these gentoo penguin groups can be shown to belong to different species.
questions.answer: Test whether they can interbreed to produce fertile offspring, or compare their DNA.
steps: Species are groups that cannot produce fertile offspring with each other.
Breeding the penguins from different groups together tests this.
Alternatively compare DNA sequences; large differences show different species.
Either test would show whether the groups are separate species.

questions.question: Explain how different species of gentoo penguin could have formed, using the map of four island groups.
questions.answer: Geographic isolation on separate island groups stops gene flow; different conditions and mutations lead to divergence until reproductive isolation occurs.
steps: Penguin populations became geographically isolated on separate island groups.
Gene flow between the groups stopped.
Each group experienced different conditions, causing different selection pressures.
Mutations and natural selection led to genetic divergence in each group.
Over time the groups became reproductively isolated and formed separate species.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term organ.
questions.answer: A structure made of several different tissues working together to perform a specific function.
steps: Cells group into tissues of one type.
Tissues of different types combine to form an organ.
The tissues work together for a specific function.
Examples include leaves and roots in plants.

questions.question: Which organelle is labelled X in the photograph of part of a cell? A chloroplast B endoplasmic reticulum C Golgi apparatus D plasmodesmata.
questions.answer: B: endoplasmic reticulum
steps: X points to stacks of long, parallel membranes (flattened sacs) packed closely around the outside of the nucleus.
This is the endoplasmic reticulum (rough ER, connected with the nuclear envelope and studded with ribosomes).
A chloroplast has grana and a double membrane, the Golgi apparatus is a stack of curved sacs with vesicles, and plasmodesmata are channels through the cell wall, so only B fits.

questions.question: Give the name and function of the organelle that contains the nucleolus.
questions.answer: Nucleus; it stores DNA and controls the cell's activities by controlling transcription.
steps: The nucleolus is found inside the nucleus.
The nucleus stores the cell's DNA as chromosomes.
It controls gene expression by controlling transcription.
So the organelle is the nucleus.

questions.question: Which are functions of the nucleolus? 1 production of ribosomes; 2 synthesis of DNA; 3 synthesis of RNA. A 1 and 2 only B 1 and 3 only C 2 and 3 only D 1, 2 and 3.
questions.answer: B 1 and 3 only
steps: The nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits, so function 1 is correct.
It transcribes rRNA, so function 3 is correct.
DNA synthesis (replication) happens in the nucleus as a whole, not in the nucleolus, so function 2 is wrong.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: State which of the three domains would contain an organism with organelles X and Y, where Y is the organelle containing the nucleolus.
questions.answer: Eukarya.
steps: Y is the nucleus, which has a nucleolus.
Only eukaryotic cells have a nucleus with a nucleolus.
Prokaryotes lack a nucleus.
So the domain is Eukarya.

questions.question: Which structure in the cells of potato tubers would store starch molecules? A amyloplast B chloroplast C middle lamella D vacuole.
questions.answer: A amyloplast
steps: Amyloplasts are plastids specialised for storing starch.
Chloroplasts make sugars by photosynthesis, but tubers are underground and do not photosynthesise.
The middle lamella is the layer between cell walls and does not store starch.
So the answer is A, amyloplast.

questions.question: Explain how the structure of starch enables potato tubers to have a high energy content.
questions.answer: Starch is compact and insoluble, storing many glucose units in a small space that can be hydrolysed to release energy.
steps: Starch is made of many glucose units joined together.
Its compact, coiled structure stores a large amount of glucose in a small volume.
Being insoluble, it does not affect the water potential of the cell.
Hydrolysis releases glucose, which is respired to release a lot of energy.

questions.question: Describe one piece of information needed to determine if the Akhal-Teke is the same breed as the Turkoman horse, and give a reason.
questions.answer: DNA or genetic information; if the sequences match, or they interbreed with fertile offspring, they are the same breed.
steps: Collect DNA samples from Akhal-Teke and Turkoman horses.
Compare genetic information such as base sequences of marker genes.
Very similar genetic information suggests they are the same breed.
Reason: breeds that are genetically identical or interbreed freely are not separate breeds.

questions.question: A population of 5457 Akhal-Teke horses has a heterozygosity index of 0.661. How many are heterozygotes? A 1 850 B 3 607 C 5 457 D 8 255.
steps: Heterozygotes = H x total = 0.661 x 5457.
This is about 3607 horses, matching option B.
Options A, C and D do not match this calculation.

questions.question: Suggest one reason why the Caspian breed has small hooves but the Arabian has large hooves in proportion to mass.
questions.answer: Caspian horses live on rocky mountain terrain where small hooves give grip, while large hooves spread weight on the sand of the Arabian desert.
steps: Caspian horses live in mountainous, rocky regions.
Small hooves suit hard, rocky ground and rough slopes.
Arabian horses live in sandy deserts, where large hooves spread the body weight.
Large hooves stop the horse sinking into the sand.

questions.question: Complete the table showing how many of 400 Caspian horses are heterozygous and how many are homozygous recessive for one gene, using p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1.
questions.answer: Heterozygous: 179 horses; two copies of the recessive allele: 175 horses.
steps: Number heterozygous = 0.448 x 400 = 179 and number homozygous recessive = 0.437 x 400 = 175 (check: 46 + 179 + 175 = 400).

questions.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using frozen sperm in breeding programmes for the Akhal-Teke and Caspian breeds, using the table and graph.
questions.answer: Frozen sperm keeps the genes of dead males and can keep genetic diversity in the breeding programmes, but fewer frozen sperm can swim and survive for less time, so fewer pregnancies result.
steps: Advantage: sperm from males that have died can still be used, so their alleles are kept in the population and the genetic diversity is higher (reducing inbreeding in small populations such as the Akhal-Teke); sperm can be stored for a long time and moved without moving the animals.

Disadvantage: freezing and thawing lowers the percentage of sperm that can swim (from 50.7% to 26.9%, 47% fewer), sperm survival time (from 117.7 to 48.5 hours, 59% less) and increases the percentage with damaged DNA (28.7% to 39.3%), which may cause mutations or failed development.

The graph shows a strong positive correlation (r = +0.90) between the percentage of sperm that can swim and the percentage of successful pregnancies (about 0% at 10% swimming to 80 to 100% at 40 to 50%), so the lower swimming ability of frozen sperm (27%) means fewer successful pregnancies (about 40% from the line, against nearly 100% at 50%).

Correlation does not prove cause, and the data are for a limited number of samples (the graph has only about 15 points), so the exact figures for the horse breeds are uncertain; to overcome the problem more frozen sperm or artificial insemination could be used, and for rare breeds with small populations a lower pregnancy rate may still be better than no breeding.

questions.question: State the domain that contains diatoms.
questions.answer: Eukarya.
steps: Diatoms have a nucleus and mitochondria.
These are membrane-bound organelles found only in eukaryotic cells.
Prokaryotes do not have a nucleus or mitochondria.
So diatoms are in the Eukarya domain.

questions.question: Name two processes that take place in the nucleus of a diatom, which contains DNA.
questions.answer: DNA replication and transcription.
steps: DNA replication copies the DNA before cell division.
Transcription makes mRNA (and rRNA) from a DNA template.
Both happen inside the nucleus.
Either two of these processes earn the marks.

questions.question: Describe how a decrease in biodiversity within an ocean habitat could be determined.
questions.answer: Sample the habitat repeatedly, compare species richness, and calculate and compare the index of diversity over time.
steps: Take samples from the same ocean site using the same method each time.
Count the number of different species to find species richness.
Calculate the index of diversity from the number of individuals of each species.
A fall in species richness or index of diversity over time shows biodiversity has decreased.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term endemic, as applied to the Javanese edelweiss plant.
questions.answer: Found naturally only in one country or region (here Indonesia) and nowhere else.
steps: Endemic means a species is restricted to one geographic area.
The Javanese edelweiss is found naturally only in Indonesia.
It does not occur naturally in other countries.
So endemic means restricted to this one region.

questions.question: Using a graticule where 100 divisions is 0.1 mm, which is the length of the pollen grain? A 2.3 mm B 23 micrometres C 230 micrometres D 2300 nm.
questions.answer: B: 23 micrometres
steps: Read the pollen grain on the eyepiece graticule: it extends from about 28 to about 51 divisions, a length of about 23 divisions.
100 divisions = 0.1 mm = 100 um, so 1 division = 1 um.
Length = 23 divisions x 1 um = 23 um (B).

questions.question: State what is meant by the term magnification.
questions.answer: How many times larger the image of an object is than the actual size of the object.
steps: Magnification is the ratio of image size to actual size.
It is found by dividing image size by actual size.
A magnification of 100 means the image is 100 times larger.
It describes how much bigger a view appears under a microscope.

questions.question: Describe the roles of the tube nucleus and the generative nucleus in a germinating pollen grain.
questions.answer: The tube nucleus controls growth of the pollen tube; the generative nucleus divides to form two male nuclei that fertilise the egg and polar nuclei.
steps: The tube nucleus controls the growth of the pollen tube.
It sits at the front of the tube and guides its growth towards the ovule.
The generative nucleus divides by mitosis to form two male gamete nuclei.
One male nucleus fuses with the egg to form the zygote, and the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form the endosperm.

questions.question: Describe the role of the rough endoplasmic reticulum in the formation of extracellular enzymes.
questions.answer: Ribosomes on the RER make the enzyme proteins, which enter the RER lumen and are transported in vesicles to the Golgi for processing and secretion.
steps: Ribosomes attached to the RER translate mRNA into polypeptide chains.
The polypeptides enter the lumen of the RER and fold into enzymes.
Vesicles bud off the RER and carry the enzymes to the Golgi apparatus.
The Golgi modifies and packages the enzymes, and vesicles release them from the cell by exocytosis.

questions.question: Using the graph of percentage loss in mass of wood blocks for species A and B, comment on the results.
questions.answer: Species A breaks down wood much faster than species B: the mass loss increases with time for both, reaching about 83% for A but only about 16% for B at 16 weeks.
steps: Both species cause a greater loss in mass of the wood as time increases, so both break it down.
Species A: about 15% at 4 weeks, 41% at 8 weeks, 52% at 12 weeks and 83% at 16 weeks, so more than 5 times that of B at the end.
Species B: about 3% at 4 weeks, 11% at 8 weeks, 15% at 12 weeks and 16% at 16 weeks, so B slows down and almost levels off after 12 weeks.

The error bars for the two species do not overlap at any time (for example at 8 weeks A has 24 to 55 and B has 6 to 15), so the difference is probably significant, although the error bars for A are large at 8 and 12 weeks, so there is much variation between blocks.

questions.question: Suggest one reason for the difference in breakdown of wood by species A and species B.
questions.answer: The two species produce different extracellular enzymes, so they break down different molecules in the wood.
steps: Different fungal species have different genes.
Their genes code for different extracellular enzymes.
Different enzymes hydrolyse different molecules such as lignin or cellulose.
So the species differ in how much wood they break down.

questions.question: Using the table of data for habitat two and the index of diversity formula, calculate the index of diversity for habitat two.
steps: Fill in the missing value for species C: n(n - 1) = 27 x 26 = 702.

questions.question: State which habitat has the higher biodiversity, giving a reason.
questions.answer: Habitat one, because its index of diversity (4.2) is higher than that of habitat two (3.1).
steps: A higher index of diversity means that there are more species and that the individuals are more evenly spread among them.
Habitat one has D = 4.2 and habitat two has D = 3.1, so habitat one has the higher biodiversity (habitat two is dominated by species G with 120 of 231 individuals).

questions.question: Explain the processes a seed bank could use to conserve endangered plant species D.
questions.answer: Collect seeds from many plants, dry and freeze them for storage, and test viability by germination so stock can be regrown.
steps: Collect seeds from many individual plants to capture genetic diversity.
Dry the seeds to reduce water content.
Store the dry seeds frozen at low temperature to slow metabolism.
Test viability by germinating samples regularly and grow plants to replenish the stock.

questions.question: Which term describes the subspecies of island fox found only on Santa Cruz? A diversity B endemic C mutation D specific.
questions.answer: B endemic
steps: Endemic means found in only one restricted area.
The fox subspecies is found only on Santa Cruz.
Mutation is a change in DNA, not a location term.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: Explain how isolation caused the formation of six fox populations with different characteristics.
questions.answer: Islands isolated the populations, stopping gene flow; mutation and different selection pressures on each island made them diverge.
steps: The six islands are separated by sea, so fox populations are geographically isolated.
Gene flow between islands is prevented.
Each island has different conditions and selection pressures.
Mutations and natural selection on each island produced different characteristics over time.

questions.question: Explain how molecular evidence could determine which of the other five fox populations is most closely related to the Santa Cruz fox population.
questions.answer: Compare DNA base sequences of each population with the Santa Cruz fox; the most similar sequence is the most closely related.
steps: Extract DNA from each fox population.
Compare the base sequences of the same gene with the Santa Cruz fox.
Count the differences in base sequences.
The population with the fewest differences is the most closely related.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage decrease in the Santa Cruz fox population from 1994 to 2002, using the graph.
steps: Santa Cruz is the dashed line: about 1500 foxes in 1994 and about 80 in 2002.
Percentage decrease = 1420 / 1500 x 100 = 94.7%, about 95%.

questions.question: Explain how the Hardy-Weinberg equation can show the change in frequency of a recessive allele in the Santa Cruz population from 1994 to 2000.
questions.answer: Count recessive homozygotes in each year, find q from q^2 for each year, and compare the q values.
steps: Count the number of recessive phenotype foxes in the population in 1994.
Calculate q^2 as this fraction, then q as its square root.
Repeat for 2000.
Comparing the two q values shows whether the recessive allele frequency has changed.

questions.question: Explain how conservation could increase the sizes of the Santa Cruz and Santa Catalina fox populations while maintaining their genetic diversity.
questions.answer: Captive breeding and controlled releases raise numbers, and moving foxes between islands with managed breeding maintains genetic diversity.
steps: Captive breeding can increase the population size of each fox population.
Breeding programmes can be managed to avoid inbreeding and keep alleles.
Moving individuals between the Santa Cruz and Santa Catalina populations allows gene flow.
Reducing predation by golden eagles and disease from dogs and raccoons protects the population.

questions.question: Explain why the body cells of the mother and baby Malayan tapir have genetic similarities and differences.
questions.answer: The baby inherits half its alleles from each parent, so it shares many alleles with the mother but gets different combinations from the father.
steps: The baby is formed when a sperm and egg fuse, combining two haploid gametes.
The baby shares many alleles with the mother, because half its chromosomes come from her.
The other half come from the father, so differences arise from different alleles.
Random assortment and crossing over during meiosis make each gamete, and so each baby, genetically unique.

questions.question: Which equation can be used to calculate the heterozygosity index? Options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: A: heterozygosity index = number of heterozygotes / number of individuals in the population
steps: The heterozygosity index is the proportion of individuals in the population that are heterozygous for a gene.
So it is the number of heterozygotes divided by the number of individuals in the population, which is A (the others use the number of species or are the wrong way up).

questions.question: Explain how scientists could determine whether the frequency of the recessive allele in the Malayan tapir is changing over time.
questions.answer: Count recessive homozygotes at different times, calculate q from q^2, and compare the values over time.
steps: Count the number of recessive homozygous tapirs in samples taken at different times.
Calculate q^2 for each sample and then q.
Compare q values over time.
A change in q shows that the allele frequency is changing.

questions.question: Give one similarity between the current and earlier distribution of the Malayan tapir shown in the map.
questions.answer: The current distribution lies inside the earlier distribution: it is in the same regions (Thailand, the Malay peninsula and Sumatra) and is a narrow strip running along the same direction.
steps: Every area of current distribution (dark grey) lies within the area of the earlier distribution (light grey), so the tapirs are found in the same general areas as before.
In both cases the distribution is found in Thailand, the Malay peninsula and Sumatra but not in Cambodia or Vietnam.

questions.question: Suggest one reason why human activity has caused the distribution of the Malayan tapir to reduce.
questions.answer: Deforestation and habitat loss for farming, roads and development.
steps: Forests are cleared for agriculture such as palm oil plantations.
Development and roads fragment the forest.
The tapir loses its habitat and food supply.
So its range shrinks.

questions.question: Explain how a captive breeding programme could maintain the genetic diversity of Malayan tapir populations that have been separated.
questions.answer: Breed tapirs from different populations in a managed studbook, avoiding inbreeding, then release them to increase gene flow.
steps: Animals from different isolated populations are brought together in captivity.
A studbook records parentage so breeding pairs are unrelated.
This avoids inbreeding and keeps a wide range of alleles.
Offspring can be released into the wild to restore gene flow between populations.

questions.question: Migration is an example of which type of adaptation? A anatomical B behavioural C isolational D physiological.
questions.answer: B behavioural
steps: Migration is a behaviour, moving between regions at set times.
Anatomical adaptations are physical structures.
Physiological adaptations are internal processes like metabolism.
So the answer is B, behavioural.

questions.question: The heterozygosity index for a cluster of 8000 Monarch butterflies is 0.166. Calculate the number of heterozygotes.
steps: Heterozygotes = H x total number of individuals.
This is a whole number of butterflies.
So there are 1328 heterozygotes.

questions.question: Explain the effect of increased glyphosate herbicide use on Monarch butterfly populations and their genetic diversity after 2010, using the graph of milkweed fields.
questions.answer: Milkweed is the only food of the caterpillars, and the graph shows its fields fell from 100% in 1999 to about 18% in 2010, so fewer monarchs survive and breed; the population falls and loses genetic diversity.
steps: Female monarchs lay their eggs on milkweed, and the caterpillars feed on it, so the glyphosate that kills milkweed removes food and egg-laying sites.

The graph shows the percentage of fields containing milkweed fell from 100% (1999) to about 40% (2005) and about 18% (2010), a fall of more than 80%, so after 2010 even fewer caterpillars would survive to adulthood and the monarch population would continue to decline.

A smaller population means a smaller gene pool: alleles are lost by genetic drift (a genetic bottleneck), there is more inbreeding and so the genetic diversity (the heterozygosity index) falls, which reduces the ability to adapt to disease or change and could lead to extinction.

questions.question: State what is meant by polygenic inheritance with reference to the egg-laying rate of hens.
questions.answer: Egg-laying rate is controlled by many genes at different loci, each with a small additive effect, giving continuous variation.
steps: Polygenic inheritance means many genes control one characteristic.
Each gene at a different locus contributes a small amount to egg-laying rate.
The combined alleles produce a range of egg-laying rates.
This gives continuous variation across the population.

questions.question: Sketch a labelled graph showing the expected egg-laying rate for a population of hens.
questions.answer: A bell-shaped (normal distribution) curve with egg-laying rate (e.g. eggs per year) on the x axis and the number of hens on the y axis, with the peak at the mean.
steps: Label the x axis "egg-laying rate (eggs per year)" and the y axis "number of hens" (frequency).
Draw a smooth, symmetrical bell-shaped curve with the peak at the mean egg-laying rate, tailing off at both ends without touching the axes, because polygenic traits show continuous variation.

questions.question: Give the name and function of the organelle shown in the photograph of a plant cell.
questions.answer: Chloroplast; it carries out photosynthesis (absorbs light and makes glucose from carbon dioxide and water).
steps: The organelle has a double membrane and contains stacks of thylakoid membranes (grana) joined by lamellae, so it is a chloroplast.
Its function is photosynthesis: the light-dependent reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes and the Calvin cycle in the stroma, making sugars.

questions.question: Name the type of microscope used for the photograph and give one reason.
questions.answer: Transmission electron microscope (TEM); it shows the internal structure (grana and membranes) in great detail because of its high resolution and magnification.
steps: The image is a flat, thin slice through the organelle, showing its internal membranes (the grana) in detail, which is typical of a transmission electron microscope.
The thylakoid membranes are only about 10 nm thick and a light microscope (resolution about 200 nm) could not show them, so an electron microscope was used (higher resolution).

questions.question: State what is meant by the term species richness.
questions.answer: The number of different species in an area or habitat.
steps: Species richness counts the different species present.
It does not depend on the number of individuals.
It is one measure of biodiversity.
So it is the number of different species.

questions.question: Using the table of individuals of each species in the lake before the pygmy weed appeared, calculate the index of diversity to two decimal places.
steps: Fill in the missing values: B: (n - 1) = 11 and n(n - 1) = 132; E: n(n - 1) = 42 (given); F: n(n - 1) = 46 x 45 = 2070.
D = 23 256 / 6042 = 3.85 (to 2 decimal places).

questions.question: A year after New Zealand pygmy weed appeared, the index of diversity was 1.8. Suggest the effect of the weed on the diversity of this part of the lake.
questions.answer: Diversity fell: the weed outcompetes native species, reducing species richness and the balance of numbers.
steps: A lower index of diversity means lower biodiversity.
The pygmy weed forms dense growth that shades and outcompetes native plants.
Native species decline or disappear as the weed takes over.
Fewer species and a less even spread of individuals lower the index of diversity.

questions.question: Identify two reasons why the Grandidier's baobab is endangered, using the information and photographs.
questions.answer: Habitat loss to rice fields, and decline of fruit bats that pollinate the trees.
steps: The baobab is endemic to Madagascar, so loss of its single range is serious.
The tree is growing in a field of rice, showing habitat is being cleared for farming.
Fruit bats transfer pollen between trees, so falling bat numbers reduce pollination.
Reduced pollination leads to fewer seeds and slower recovery of the population.

questions.question: Give two reasons how education could help conserve the Grandidier's baobab.
questions.answer: Education raises awareness so people protect the trees; it teaches sustainable farming and land use that reduces habitat loss.
steps: Education raises public awareness of the tree's value and endangered status.
Local people can learn to protect trees rather than clear them.
Farmers can be taught sustainable farming that protects habitat.
Educated people are more likely to support conservation laws and projects.

questions.question: Explain the role of one named molecule in plants that uses calcium ions.
questions.answer: Calcium pectate in the cell wall (middle lamella) cross-links pectin chains, strengthening the wall.
steps: Calcium ions bind to pectin molecules in the middle lamella and cell wall.
This forms calcium pectate, which cross-links the pectin chains.
The cross-links give the wall strength and rigidity.
So calcium pectate helps the plant cell wall resist stress.

questions.question: Which tissue would transport water down the stem of a plant? A phloem B sclerenchyma C vacuole D xylem.
questions.answer: D xylem
steps: Xylem transports water and mineral ions up the plant from the roots.
Phloem transports sugars, not water.
Sclerenchyma gives support and is not a transport tissue.
The vacuole stores water within a cell, so the answer is D, xylem.

questions.question: Give two conclusions that can be made from the graph of the mean number of pods per soybean plant with and without added magnesium ions.
questions.answer: Adding magnesium ions increased the mean number of pods per plant in both years, but the difference is only clearly significant in 2019; and the pods per plant were higher in 2020 in both fields.
steps: With magnesium the mean number of pods is higher than without in 2019 (about 98 against 87.5, 12% more) and in 2020 (about 115.5 against 106.5, 8% more), so magnesium increases the yield, as it is needed for chlorophyll and enzyme activation.

In 2019 the error bars do not overlap (about 94 to 102 against 84 to 90.5), so the difference is probably significant, but in 2020 they overlap (108 to 122 against 105 to 109), so the difference may be due to chance.
The mean number of pods was higher in 2020 than in 2019 in both fields (about 20 more), so another factor (such as the weather) also affected the number of pods.

questions.question: Comment on the results of the graph showing the effect of magnesium ions on the mass of soybeans and maize grains.
questions.answer: Magnesium ions increased the mass of 100 soybeans (about 8%) and 100 maize grains (about 4%), but the effect is clear only for soybean because the error bars for maize overlap; maize grains are about twice as heavy as soybeans.
steps: Soybean: the mass of 100 beans is about 15.5 g without magnesium and about 16.8 g with it (+8%); the error bars do not overlap (about 15 to 16.2 against 16.7 to 16.9), so the increase is probably significant.
Maize: the mass of 100 grains is about 31.2 g without and 32.5 g with magnesium (+4%); the error bars overlap (30.6 to 31.8 against 31.5 to 33.4), so the difference is not clearly significant.
Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll (more photosynthesis, so more sugar and starch to store in the seeds) and to activate enzymes, so seeds are heavier, but the increase is small in both.
The effect may differ because the two crops differ; for both, more repeats or a larger sample size would give more reliable conclusions.

questions.question: If p^2 = 0.36, which is the value of 2pq? A 0.06 B 0.16 C 0.48 D 0.64.
steps: So the answer is C, 0.48.

questions.question: Albino rabbits have genotype bb. State the part of the equation p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1 that represents this genotype.
steps: The recessive homozygous genotype bb has two recessive alleles.
Its frequency is the square of the recessive allele frequency q.
In the equation this is the q^2 term.
So the part is q^2.

questions.question: Explain how a viral disease that killed many rabbits on Lokrum Island could change allele frequencies of genes that protect against the virus.
questions.answer: Rabbits with resistance alleles survive and breed, so the resistance alleles become more common through natural selection.
steps: Rabbits vary in their alleles for virus resistance.
The virus kills rabbits without effective resistance alleles.
Resistant rabbits survive and reproduce, passing on their alleles.
The frequency of resistance alleles in the population increases over generations.

questions.question: Which labelled structure (W, X, Y or Z) in the micrograph of plant tissues is a xylem vessel?
questions.answer: C: Y
steps: Xylem vessels are large cells with thick, lignified walls and wide empty lumens.
Y points to the group of larger, darker thick-walled cells in the lower half of the vascular bundle, which is the xylem.
V is the sclerenchyma cap of small thick-walled cells, W is the phloem, X is the layer of cambium and Z is parenchyma.

questions.question: Which labelled structure (V, W, X or Y) in the micrograph contains sieve plates?
questions.answer: B: W
steps: Sieve plates are found in the sieve tube elements of the phloem.
W points to the group of small, thin-walled cells (sieve tubes and companion cells) next to the sclerenchyma cap, which is the phloem.
V is sclerenchyma, X is the cambium and Y is xylem, so none of these contains sieve plates.

questions.question: Explain the advantages for the millipede of being able to make holes in xylem and phloem tissues.
questions.answer: It gains easy access to water and sugars from the sap, a food source that needs no chewing of tough tissue.
steps: Xylem contains water and mineral ions the millipede needs.
Phloem contains sugars and amino acids, a rich energy source.
Making holes lets the millipede feed on sap without chewing tough plant tissue.
This gives reliable nutrition, which helps it survive and reproduce.

questions.question: Suggest why the Illacme tobini millipede has a hard exoskeleton and 200 poison glands.
questions.answer: The exoskeleton gives physical protection from predators, and the poison glands deter predators by making the millipede toxic.
steps: A hard exoskeleton physically protects the millipede from being bitten or crushed.
Poison glands release toxins when the millipede is attacked.
Predators that taste the poison learn to avoid it.
Both adaptations increase survival and so reproductive success.

questions.question: Explain how scientists could determine how closely related I. plenipes is to I. tobini.
questions.answer: Compare the DNA base sequences of the two species; more similar sequences mean they are more closely related.
steps: Extract DNA from both millipede species.
Sequence the same gene in each and compare the base sequences.
Count the number of differences between the sequences.
Fewer differences indicate a closer evolutionary relationship.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of a fungal cell with a bacterial cell, using the diagram of a fungal cell.
questions.answer: Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes; the fungal cell is eukaryotic with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, while the bacterial cell is prokaryotic with a nucleoid and circular DNA.
steps: Both cells have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes.
The fungal cell is eukaryotic, so it has a nucleus with linear DNA in chromosomes.
The fungal cell has membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and an ER.
The bacterial cell is prokaryotic, with no nucleus; its DNA is circular and free in the cytoplasm.
Fungal ribosomes are larger (80S) than bacterial ribosomes (70S).
The fungal cell wall contains chitin, while bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan.

questions.question: Complete a graph showing how DNA content per cell changes when a cell with 2 a.u. of DNA undergoes meiosis to produce gametes.
questions.answer: Draw a line: 2 a.u., then a rise to 4 a.u. (DNA replication), a level section at 4, a fall to 2 (end of meiosis I), a level section at 2, and a fall to 1 a.u. (end of meiosis II) at the end.
steps: Start at 2 a.u. (the line already drawn), then DNA replication in interphase doubles the content, so the line rises to 4 a.u. and stays level through the first stages of meiosis (prophase I to anaphase I).

At the end of meiosis I (when the homologous chromosomes are separated and the cell divides) the DNA content per cell halves in one vertical drop from 4 to 2 a.u., and it stays at 2 a.u. through meiosis II up to anaphase II.

At the end of meiosis II the chromatids separate and the cells divide, so the content halves again from 2 to 1 a.u., giving gametes with 1 a.u. (a haploid cell has half the DNA of the original diploid cell).
Use vertical (or steep) lines for the increases and decreases, and plateaus between them.

questions.question: The actual length of the pollen grain between X and Y is 24 micrometres. Calculate the magnification of the photograph, to two significant figures.
steps: Magnification = length of the image / actual length.
The line XY measures about 16 mm on the printed page (about 58 px at 745 px per 210 mm); a ruler measurement of 16 mm to 17 mm gives x670 to x710.
Convert: 16.3 mm = 16 300 um, so magnification = 16 300 / 24 = 680 (6.8 x 10^2).

questions.question: Describe the growth of a pollen tube and the process of fertilisation in a flower after pollen is transferred by a bee.
questions.answer: The tube grows down the style to the ovule, guided by chemicals; the generative nucleus divides, one male nucleus fuses with the egg and the other with the polar nuclei.
steps: The pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube.
The tube nucleus leads the tube down through the style, guided by chemical signals to the ovule.
The generative nucleus divides by mitosis into two male nuclei within the tube.
One male nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus to form a diploid zygote.
The other male nucleus fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.

questions.question: How many of the 418 peony plants are heterozygous for gene PS105? A 15 B 60 C 340 D 350.
steps: The heterozygosity index of PS105 is 0.036 = number of heterozygotes / number of individuals.
Number of heterozygotes = 0.036 x 418 = 15.05, which is 15 (A).

questions.question: The width of peony leaves is an example of polygenic inheritance. Which row of the table is correct for leaf width?
questions.answer: C: not one gene; determined by multiple alleles of several genes; continuous variation
steps: Polygenic inheritance means that a characteristic is controlled by several genes, so "one gene determines leaf width" is wrong (x).
Leaf width is determined by multiple alleles of several genes (tick), and polygenic characteristics show continuous variation (tick).
So the row is x, tick, tick: C.

questions.question: Suggest why the population of the St Helena plover decreased after cats and rats were introduced to the island.
questions.answer: Cats and rats eat the eggs and chicks in the ground nests, so fewer young survive.
steps: The plover lays its eggs in nests on the ground.
Cats and rats can reach ground nests easily.
They prey on eggs and chicks, so few young reach adulthood.
With fewer young surviving, the population declines.

questions.question: The plover population rose from 200 adults in 2006 to 560 in 2016. Calculate the mean rate of increase per year.
questions.answer: 36 birds per year
steps: Increase = 560 - 200 = 360 birds.
Mean rate = 360 / 10 = 36.
So the population increased by 36 birds per year.

questions.question: Describe how the St Helena breeding programme could have increased the gumwood tree population from two trees in 2009 to 6000 in 2019.
questions.answer: Collect seeds or cuttings from the two trees, grow seedlings, pollinate them by hand and plant them in protected sites.
steps: Collect seeds or cuttings from the two surviving trees.
Propagate them to grow many seedlings in a nursery.
Hand-pollinate flowers to ensure seed set and genetic mixing between parents.
Plant the young trees in protected areas where rabbits cannot reach them.

questions.question: Explain one way young gumwood trees could be protected from rabbits.
questions.answer: Surround young trees with fencing or netting so rabbits cannot reach and eat the shoots.
steps: Rabbits eat the shoots of young trees, which prevents growth.
A physical barrier such as fencing or wire mesh stops rabbits reaching the tree.
Protected trees can grow past the height where rabbits can reach.
This allows the young trees to survive and reproduce.

questions.question: Describe how a seed bank would successfully select, prepare and store seeds from St Helena gumwood trees to aid conservation.
questions.answer: Select seeds from many healthy trees for genetic diversity, dry them, store them frozen, and test viability regularly.
steps: Collect seeds from many different trees to keep genetic diversity.
Select healthy, mature seeds that are not damaged or diseased.
Dry the seeds to a low moisture content so they can be frozen safely.
Store in sealed containers at low temperature and test germination regularly.

questions.question: Using the table of data for habitat 1 and the index of diversity formula, calculate the index of diversity to two decimal places.
steps: Fill in the missing value for species E: n(n - 1) = 63 x 62 = 3906.
D = 818 120 / 566 906 = 1.44 (to 2 decimal places).

questions.question: Habitat 2 has an index of diversity of 2.80. A student says habitat 2 has higher biodiversity. State whether you agree and give a reason.
questions.answer: Agree: habitat 2 has the higher biodiversity because its index of diversity (2.80) is higher than that of habitat 1 (1.44).
steps: A higher index of diversity means more species and a more even spread of individuals among them.
Habitat 1 has D = 1.44 and is dominated by species A (747 of the 905 individuals), whereas habitat 2 has D = 2.80, so habitat 2 has the greater biodiversity.

questions.question: Describe the acrosome reaction, which is stimulated when a sperm binds to ZP3 on the zona pellucida.
questions.answer: The acrosome releases hydrolytic enzymes that digest the zona pellucida, letting the sperm reach and fuse with the egg membrane.
steps: Binding of the sperm to ZP3 triggers the acrosome to release its contents.
The acrosome releases hydrolytic enzymes such as acrosin.
These enzymes digest a path through the zona pellucida.
The sperm membrane then fuses with the egg membrane, allowing the nucleus to enter.

questions.question: Suggest why some sperm cells may not be able to bind to the receptor on the egg cell surface membrane.
questions.answer: The receptor and sperm protein must have complementary shapes; sperm from other species or with variant proteins cannot bind.
steps: Binding relies on a receptor and a sperm surface protein with complementary shapes.
Sperm from a different species have a different protein shape, so they cannot bind.
Genetic variation or mutation can change the shape of a sperm protein.
Sperm with an incorrectly shaped protein cannot bind, so fertilisation fails.

questions.question: Explain how more sperm cells are prevented from entering the egg cell after the first one fuses.
questions.answer: A fast block (membrane depolarisation) and a slow block (cortical granules hardening the zona pellucida) prevent polyspermy.
steps: Fusion of the first sperm causes a rapid change in the egg membrane potential, a fast block.
Cortical granules are released by exocytosis, hardening the zona pellucida as a slow block.
The hardened zona blocks other sperm from binding and entering.
So only one sperm fertilises the egg.

questions.question: Explain how scientists could have determined that E. viridis is more closely related to E. lucunter than to E. vanbrunti.
questions.answer: Compare DNA base sequences; E. viridis has more similar sequences to E. lucunter than to E. vanbrunti.
steps: Extract DNA from the three urchin species.
Sequence and compare the same genes in each species.
Count the base differences between E. viridis and each of the other two species.
The species with fewer differences is more closely related.

questions.question: Explain how reproductive isolation could have led to the formation of these three urchin species, using the maps and all information in the question.
questions.answer: Geographic separation prevents gene flow; divergence by mutation and selection makes gametes incompatible, so reproductive isolation forms separate species.
steps: Populations became geographically separated by distance or barriers, so they stopped interbreeding.
Gene flow between the separated populations ceased.
Each population experienced different conditions, so different alleles were selected.
Mutations accumulated independently in each population.
Sperm of one species could no longer fertilise eggs of another, a form of prezygotic reproductive isolation.
Over time these barriers became complete, forming three separate species.

questions.question: The generative nucleus divides to form two male nuclei. Which statement is correct? A one male nucleus forms the pollen tube B one male nucleus fertilises an egg nucleus to form the embryo C the male nuclei are diploid D two male nuclei fertilise a polar nucleus to form the endosperm.
questions.answer: B
steps: The pollen tube is formed by the tube nucleus, not a male nucleus, so A is wrong.
The male nuclei are haploid, so C is wrong.
One male nucleus fertilises the egg nucleus to form the zygote and embryo, so B is correct.
The endosperm forms when one male nucleus fuses with two polar nuclei, so D is wrong.

questions.question: Name the stage of meiosis when crossing over of non-sister chromatids occurs.
questions.answer: Prophase I.
steps: In prophase I homologous chromosomes pair up to form bivalents.
Non-sister chromatids are in close contact at chiasmata.
Segments of DNA are exchanged between chromatids here.
So crossing over occurs in prophase I.

questions.question: Describe two other processes that can give rise to genetic variation in the offspring of the passion flower.
questions.answer: Independent assortment of homologous chromosomes in meiosis, and random fusion of gametes at fertilisation.
steps: Independent assortment: homologous pairs line up randomly at metaphase I, mixing maternal and paternal chromosomes.
Random fertilisation: any male gamete may fuse with any female gamete, giving new combinations.
Both processes create new allele combinations in each offspring.
Either process named and described correctly earns the marks.

questions.question: Write an equation for the heterozygosity index.
questions.answer: H = number of heterozygotes / total number of individuals.
steps: Heterozygotes are individuals with two different alleles at a locus.
Count the number of heterozygous individuals.
Divide this by the total number of individuals sampled.
The result is H, a value that measures genetic diversity.

questions.question: Explain how seeds would be selected for storage in a seed bank.
questions.answer: Select seeds from many different healthy plants of the species to maintain genetic diversity, choosing viable, undamaged seeds.
steps: Collect seeds from many different plants to represent the genetic diversity of the species.
Choose healthy, mature seeds that are not damaged or diseased.
Check that seeds are viable before storing them.
Record the origin of each seed sample for future management.

questions.question: Which domains contain prokaryotic organisms? 1 Archaea 2 Bacteria 3 Eukarya. A 1 and 2 only B 1 and 3 only C 2 and 3 only D 1, 2 and 3.
questions.answer: A 1 and 2 only
steps: Archaea are prokaryotic (statement 1 correct).
Bacteria are prokaryotic (statement 2 correct).
Eukarya are eukaryotic, so statement 3 is wrong.
So the answer is A, 1 and 2 only.

questions.question: Which row gives the name and function of structure Z in the diagram of a prokaryotic cell?
questions.answer: D: cell membrane; controls what enters and leaves the cell
steps: Z points to the thin membrane just inside the cell wall (and capsule), enclosing the cytoplasm, which is the cell surface (plasma) membrane.
The cell membrane is partially permeable and controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
A capsule would be the outermost layer, and protein synthesis happens on ribosomes, so the row is D.

questions.question: Give the name and function of structure X and structure Y in the diagram of a prokaryotic cell.
questions.answer: X is a flagellum, used for movement (swimming); Y is a pilus (pili), used to attach to surfaces or other cells (and for conjugation).
steps: X is a long, wavy thread attached to the end of the cell, so it is a flagellum, and its rotation propels the cell, so it is used for movement.

Y is a group of short, thin, straight projections from the cell surface, which are pili (singular pilus); they allow the bacterium to attach to surfaces such as host cells, and to other bacteria during conjugation.

questions.question: Which structure could be found inside a prokaryotic cell? A chloroplast B linear DNA C nucleolus D ribosome.
questions.answer: D ribosome
steps: Prokaryotes lack chloroplasts, so A is wrong.
Prokaryotic DNA is circular, not linear, so B is wrong.
Prokaryotes lack a nucleus, so there is no nucleolus (C is wrong).
Ribosomes are present in prokaryotes (70S), so the answer is D.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term resolution, for an electron microscope with resolution of 2 nm.
questions.answer: The smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as two separate points.
steps: Resolution is the ability to distinguish two objects that are close together.
It is the minimum separation at which two points can be seen as separate.
A resolution of 2 nm means points less than 2 nm apart cannot be distinguished.
Better resolution means a smaller value and more detail.

questions.question: Cell P has a diameter of 0.60 (units as in the question) and the volume formula is given in the question. Calculate its volume to two decimal places.
steps: The diameter is 0.60 um, so the radius is r = 0.30 um.
V = 0.1131 um^3, which is 0.11 um^3 to two decimal places.
